title: Beyond Body Image
text:
What this book is
This book does three things at once. It is an academic essay on the environmental conditions in which feeding and eating disorders arise in adolescence. It is a practical guide for health and education professionals. And it offers an interactive toolkit: a set of calibrated prompt sequences for large language models (LLMs) that help adults organise what they have noticed and take it to the right professional.
Its focus is avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID). ARFID was added to the diagnostic manuals in 2013 (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), and it does not fit the story that dominates public debate on young people, social media and eating. That story is about body image. ARFID, by definition, is not.
crumbs: Preface

title: Beyond Body Image
text:
Why “beyond body image”
Most research and policy on social media and eating disorders follows a single pathway: exposure to appearance ideals, social comparison, body dissatisfaction, then restriction (Dane & Bhatia, 2023; Holland & Tiggemann, 2016). The pathway is real and well documented. It is also partial. Children and adolescents can restrict food for reasons that have nothing to do with their bodies: food can feel or taste intolerable, eating can hold no interest, or a single frightening episode of choking or vomiting can make eating feel unsafe (Bryant-Waugh et al., 2022; Zickgraf & Ellis, 2018).
Instruments built to detect weight and shape concerns are, in this respect, like smoke detectors in a house with a gas leak: sensitive, reliable and silent about the hazard that matters. In a validation study with Turkish adolescents, ARFID subscales were largely unrelated to weight- and shape-related eating attitudes (Çelik et al., 2026). This book asks what follows, scientifically and practically, when we take that silence seriously.

title: Beyond Body Image
text:
Conventions

Each chapter opens with an In plain words box: a short summary in accessible language.
Claims about the evidence carry a grade where the evidence is thin or contested: E1 systematic or meta-analytic evidence; E2 several consistent primary studies; E3 single studies, case reports or cross-sectional associations; H hypothesis with mechanistic plausibility only.
Clinical terms are given in British English, with Spanish equivalents in the Glossary.
Every figure states its source in author–date form. Simulations are labelled as such; their code can be unfolded beneath the text, and the numbers quoted from them are computed when the book is rendered.
Searches and web sources are dated. Helplines on the If you are worried page were checked on the date shown there.
Following safe-communication practice, the book gives no figures for weight, calories or portions, and no images of bodies.
crumbs: Preface

title: Beyond Body Image
text:
What this book is not
It is not a diagnostic instrument and does not replace assessment by a qualified professional. The toolkit does not score, label or store anything. Software that is intended to support diagnostic decisions falls under medical-device regulation in the European Union (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2017); this book deliberately stays on the other side of that line.

title: Beyond Body Image
text:
How this book was made
The book was written with the assistance of a large language model, used for literature retrieval, drafting, data analysis and code, and for the bilingual terminology work shared with the translat-ia workshop. Every source was checked against its primary record, bibliographic metadata for indexed articles were generated programmatically from PubMed, and the author takes full responsibility for the content. The same principle the book applies to its toolkit (the model as scribe, not judge) applied to its writing.

This initiative of the Computational Humanities and Social Sciences Unit examines the intersection of artificial intelligence, language, translation and society through interdisciplinary seminars and workshops.
I am grateful to Carmen Moreno, a student on the Doctoral Programme in Languages, Texts and Contexts at the University of Granada, for her dedication to developing professional competence of the highest level in specialised translation. The need for expert professionals is evident in most of the content on health, asylum and the courts that people from different cultures and with different levels of literacy consult online every day. Errors and biases in information of this kind have potentially serious and often irreversible consequences, so human oversight of such content and of its multilingual dissemination should be among the binding criteria of corporate responsibility for public and private institutions alike. I hope that the efforts of the thousands of undergraduate and postgraduate translation students who view the arrival of advanced AI tools and systems with misgiving and uncertainty will prove worthwhile. Such systems may emulate certain aspects of expert human competence, but they can hardly ensure, let alone guarantee, the quality of their output without human supervision and verification.

title: If you are worried · Si te preocupa
text:
EnglishEspañol



This page is for you if…
…you are a parent, carer, teacher or young person and you have noticed that eating has become very limited, difficult or worrying. You do not need to be sure that something is wrong to read on, and you do not need a diagnosis to ask for help.


Eating difficulties are not only about weight
Some people eat a very small range of foods because certain textures, smells or tastes feel unbearable. Some rarely feel hungry or interested in food. Some are afraid that eating will make them choke, be sick or feel pain, sometimes after a frightening experience. When this starts to affect health, growth, energy, school or time with friends, it is worth talking to a professional. One name for this pattern is ARFID (avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder).
Other eating disorders do involve strong worries about weight or body shape. Both kinds of difficulty deserve help, and both are treatable. “Not about weight” does not mean “not serious”.


Signs worth talking about

The list of foods someone will eat keeps getting shorter.
Meals take a very long time, or cause distress, arguments or tears.
Avoiding eating with others: at school, with friends, at family events.
Tiredness, losing weight, or a child not growing as expected.
Relying on drinks or supplements in place of meals.
Strong worries about weight, body shape or “getting fat” (also worth discussing).



What you can do

Write down what you have noticed: when it started, which foods are accepted or avoided, what seems to make eating hard, and what happens at mealtimes.
Book an appointment with your family doctor (GP) or your child’s paediatrician and take your notes with you.
Talk to school: a tutor, school counsellor or school nurse can add useful observations.
If it helps, use the note composer in the toolkit to organise your observations. It does not give a diagnosis and it does not store anything.



While you wait for an appointment

Keep mealtimes as calm as you can. Pressure, punishments and bribes around food tend to make things harder, not easier.
Keep offering the foods the person eats now, so that they keep eating. Leave changes to the plan you agree with a professional.
Do not start a diet or cut out foods because of something seen online, unless a doctor has advised it.
Look after yourself too. Caring for someone who finds eating hard is tiring. The organisations listed below offer support for parents and carers, including groups specifically for ARFID.



If this is about you
If eating feels hard for you (because of how food feels, because you are rarely hungry, or because you are scared of what might happen), you are not being difficult and you are not alone. Tell an adult you trust: a parent, a teacher, a school nurse or your doctor. If talking is hard, you can show them this page. You can also call a helpline for young people (below); calls are free and confidential.


When it cannot wait
Seek urgent medical help today if someone faints or feels very dizzy, has chest pain or a racing or irregular heartbeat, cannot keep food or fluids down or refuses to drink, seems confused or very weak, or talks about wanting to harm themselves. If you think a life is in danger, call the emergency number now.

Spain: 112 (emergencies) · 024 (suicide-related crises, free, 24 hours)
United Kingdom: 999 (emergencies) · 111 (urgent medical advice) · Samaritans 116 123

This list is a short summary for families. Professionals use fuller guidance, such as the Royal College of Psychiatrists’ Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders (MEED), which includes summary sheets for families and carers, and the NICE guideline on eating disorders (NG69).


Where to find support
Spain

Fundación ANAR: helpline for children and adolescents 900 20 20 10 (free, confidential, 24 hours; also chat at anar.org); line for families and schools 600 50 51 52.
FEACAB, the Spanish federation of eating-disorder associations: feacab.org.
ADANER, association for people affected by eating disorders and their families, with branches in several regions: adaner.org.
ACAB, association against anorexia and bulimia (Catalonia): acab.org.

United Kingdom

Beat, the UK’s eating disorder charity, with helplines for all ages and support for carers of young people with ARFID: England 0808 801 0677 · Scotland 0808 801 0432 · Wales 0808 801 0433 · Northern Ireland 0808 801 0434 (beateatingdisorders.org.uk; opening hours on the website).
ARFID Awareness UK, a registered charity dedicated to ARFID: arfidawarenessuk.org.
Childline (for children and young people under 19; free, confidential, 24 hours): 0800 1111.

Last checked: 22 November 2026. Numbers and services can change; please check the organisation’s website.


What this site does not do
It does not diagnose, it does not replace a professional, and it does not collect or store any information you type.




Esta página es para ti si…
…eres madre, padre, cuidador/a, docente o joven y has notado que la alimentación se ha vuelto muy limitada, difícil o preocupante. No hace falta estar seguro de que algo va mal para seguir leyendo, ni tener un diagnóstico para pedir ayuda.


Las dificultades con la comida no siempre tienen que ver con el peso
Hay personas que comen muy pocos alimentos porque algunas texturas, olores o sabores les resultan insoportables. Otras casi nunca sienten hambre ni interés por la comida. Otras tienen miedo de atragantarse, vomitar o sentir dolor al comer, a veces después de una experiencia que las asustó. Cuando esto empieza a afectar a la salud, al crecimiento, a la energía, a los estudios o a la vida con amistades, conviene consultarlo con un profesional. Uno de los nombres de este patrón es ARFID (trastorno de evitación/restricción de la ingesta de alimentos).
Otros trastornos de la conducta alimentaria sí implican una fuerte preocupación por el peso o la figura. Ambos tipos de dificultad merecen ayuda y ambos tienen tratamiento. «No tiene que ver con el peso» no significa «no es grave».


Señales que conviene comentar

La lista de alimentos que acepta va siendo cada vez más corta.
Las comidas se alargan mucho o generan angustia, discusiones o llanto.
Evita comer con otras personas: en el centro educativo, con amistades, en reuniones familiares.
Cansancio, pérdida de peso o un niño o niña que no crece como se esperaba.
Sustituye comidas por bebidas o suplementos.
Fuerte preocupación por el peso, la figura o «engordar» (también conviene comentarlo).



Qué puedes hacer

Anota lo que has observado: cuándo empezó, qué alimentos acepta o evita, qué parece dificultar la comida y qué ocurre en las comidas.
Pide cita con tu médico/a de familia o con el pediatra de tu centro de salud y lleva tus notas.
Habla con el centro educativo: tutoría, departamento de orientación o enfermería escolar pueden aportar observaciones útiles.
Si te ayuda, usa el compositor de notas de la caja de herramientas para ordenar lo que has observado. No da un diagnóstico y no guarda nada.



Mientras esperas la cita

Procura que las comidas sean lo más tranquilas posible. La presión, los castigos y los premios en torno a la comida suelen complicar las cosas, no facilitarlas.
Sigue ofreciendo los alimentos que ahora come, para que siga comiendo. Deja los cambios para el plan que acordéis con un profesional.
No empieces una dieta ni elimines alimentos por algo visto en internet, salvo que lo indique un médico.
Cuida también de ti. Acompañar a alguien a quien le cuesta comer agota. Las organizaciones que aparecen más abajo ofrecen apoyo a familias y cuidadores.



Si esto va de ti
Si comer te resulta difícil (por cómo es la comida, porque casi nunca tienes hambre o porque te da miedo lo que pueda pasar), no estás siendo difícil y no eres la única persona a la que le pasa. Cuéntaselo a una persona adulta de confianza: tu madre, tu padre, un profesor o profesora, la enfermera escolar o tu médico. Si te cuesta hablar, puedes enseñarle esta página. También puedes llamar a una línea de ayuda para jóvenes (más abajo); la llamada es gratuita y confidencial.


Cuando no puede esperar
Busca atención médica urgente hoy si la persona se desmaya o se marea mucho, tiene dolor en el pecho o el corazón muy acelerado o irregular, no tolera la comida o los líquidos o se niega a beber, parece confusa o muy débil, o habla de hacerse daño. Si crees que hay una vida en peligro, llama ahora al número de emergencias.

España: 112 (emergencias) · 024 (línea de atención a la conducta suicida, gratuita, 24 horas)
Reino Unido: 999 (emergencias) · 111 (consejo médico urgente) · Samaritans 116 123

Esta lista es un resumen breve para familias. Los profesionales utilizan guías más completas, como la del Royal College of Psychiatrists sobre urgencias médicas en los trastornos de la conducta alimentaria (MEED), que incluye resúmenes para familias y cuidadores, y la guía del NICE sobre trastornos de la conducta alimentaria (NG69) (ambas en inglés).


Dónde encontrar apoyo
España

Fundación ANAR: teléfono de ayuda a niños, niñas y adolescentes 900 20 20 10 (gratuito, confidencial, 24 horas; también chat en anar.org); teléfono de la familia y los centros escolares 600 50 51 52.
FEACAB, Federación Española de Asociaciones de Ayuda y Lucha contra la Anorexia y la Bulimia: feacab.org.
ADANER, Asociación en Defensa de la Atención a la Anorexia Nerviosa y la Bulimia, con delegaciones en varias comunidades: adaner.org.
ACAB, Associació contra l’Anorèxia i la Bulímia (Cataluña): acab.org.

Reino Unido

Beat, organización benéfica británica sobre trastornos de la conducta alimentaria, con líneas de ayuda para todas las edades y apoyo a cuidadores de jóvenes con ARFID: Inglaterra 0808 801 0677 · Escocia 0808 801 0432 · Gales 0808 801 0433 · Irlanda del Norte 0808 801 0434 (beateatingdisorders.org.uk; horarios en su web).
ARFID Awareness UK, organización benéfica dedicada al ARFID: arfidawarenessuk.org.
Childline (para menores de 19 años; gratuito, confidencial, 24 horas): 0800 1111.

Última comprobación: 22 de noviembre de 2026. Los números y servicios pueden cambiar; consulta la web de cada organización.


Lo que este sitio no hace

title: Introduction
text:
A blind spot in a crowded field
A frame decides what is in the picture. It also decides, silently, what is not. Public and scientific discussion of young people, social media and eating has been organised by a powerful frame for two decades: exposure to idealised bodies leads to comparison, comparison to dissatisfaction with one’s own body, and dissatisfaction to dieting and disordered eating (Dane & Bhatia, 2023; Holland & Tiggemann, 2016). The frame is not wrong. Meta-analyses find that online appearance comparison is substantially associated with body-image concern and eating-disorder symptoms (Bonfanti et al., 2025), experiments show that idealised and “fitspiration” images increase body dissatisfaction in the short term (Fioravanti et al., 2022), and audits and internal company research show that recommender systems deliver more eating-disorder-related content to young users who signal vulnerability (Center for Countering Digital Hate, 2022; Horwitz, 2025). 4  Digital soil: social platforms, recommender systems and ARFID reviews this evidence in detail.
What the frame leaves out is restriction that has nothing to do with the body. Since 2013, the diagnostic manuals have recognised avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID): eating so restricted in range or amount that it causes weight loss or faltering growth, nutritional deficiency, dependence on supplements or marked interference with daily life, without the concern about weight or shape that defines anorexia nervosa (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Three presentations are usually described: avoidance based on the sensory characteristics of food, lack of interest in eating, and fear of aversive consequences such as choking or vomiting (Zickgraf & Ellis, 2018). They frequently combine (Three dials rather than three boxes).
ARFID is not rare, although how common it is depends heavily on how one counts. A pre-registered meta-analysis of 26 studies found that weighting studies by their methodological quality lowered the pooled prevalence estimate from 11.14% to 4.51% (Nicholls-Clow et al., 2024), and 1  Counting a moving target: context and prevalence shows why estimates from clinical caseloads, registers, population surveys and screening questionnaires differ by two orders of magnitude. It is strongly heritable, with a twin-based heritability of 0.79 (Dinkler et al., 2023), which, as 3  Seed and soil: genetic and environmental determinants explains, says nothing against the importance of environments and nothing against treatment. And it does not always respect the frame’s boundaries: a nine-year-old with ARFID and severe malnutrition could value thinness, absorbed from social media, while restricting for entirely different reasons (Barney et al., 2022).
The thesis of this book follows. Environments shape feeding and eating disorders through more than one pathway. Attending only to the body-image pathway produces a systematic blind spot, in research, in clinical recognition and in regulation. Any AI-assisted tool built on that frame will inherit the blind spot and may automate it.
crumbs: Introduction

title: Introduction
text:
Why now
Three developments make the argument timely. The first is the growth of ARFID research itself. PubMed records naming ARFID in their title or abstract numbered close to a thousand by November 2026 (How little light: a bibliometric check), and large genetic and registry cohorts are under way (Bulik et al., 2023; Hog et al., 2025). Yet almost none of this work examines digital environments: of 14 records combining ARFID with social-media terms, none reported an ARFID-specific analysis of digital exposure (Table 4.2).
The second is that generative AI is already where worried adults and young people take their questions. One psychiatrist has argued that therapy-like conversation has become the single most frequent reason people use AI (Frances, 2026). Rule-based chatbots have shown modest benefits for eating-disorder prevention in a randomised trial (Fitzsimmons-Craft et al., 2022), but general-purpose chatbots have repeatedly produced restrictive diets, concealment advice and other harmful content when tested with eating-disorder prompts (Center for Countering Digital Hate, 2023, 2025), and generative dietary advice in adolescent and eating-disorder scenarios has mixed sound guidance with restrictive recommendations (Tumanggor et al., 2026). None of these evaluations concerns ARFID.
The third is a regulatory moment. The European Union’s AI Act, amended in July 2026 by the Digital Omnibus on AI, sets out when AI systems used in health count as high-risk and when those obligations apply (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2024, 2026). Guidelines under the Digital Services Act now ask platforms to design recommender systems with minors’ safety in mind (European Commission, 2025), and Australia has begun enforcing a minimum age for social media accounts, with early evaluation data already published (eSafety Commissioner, 2026). Decisions are being taken now about which content categories count as harmful and which tools count as medical. If ARFID is absent from the evidence on which those decisions rest, it will be absent from the decisions.
crumbs: Introduction

title: Introduction
text:
Argument and structure
The book has two parts. Part I, The landscape, establishes what is known about ARFID. 1  Counting a moving target: context and prevalence asks how many people are affected and how we know, using the image of a coastline whose length depends on the ruler used to measure it, and draws from the arithmetic of screening a principle that runs through the book: a tool used mainly by people without the disorder must route people to assessment rather than label them. 2  A family of difficulties: related disorders, ages and groups places ARFID within the family of feeding and eating disorders, treats its three presentations as dials rather than boxes, and identifies the groups in which risk is concentrated: autistic young people and those with ADHD, anxious young people, and those with gastrointestinal and other chronic conditions. 3  Seed and soil: genetic and environmental determinants takes up genes and environments through the image of seed and soil, explains what a high heritability does and does not imply, and proposes a working model in which environments act less on liability than as triggers and maintaining loops.
Part II, Digital environments and generative AI, turns from what is known to what is not. 4  Digital soil: social platforms, recommender systems and ARFID reviews the evidence on social media and eating, shows by a reproducible bibliometric check how little of it reaches ARFID, and proposes seven candidate digital pathways (from vicarious fear learning to the advice parents meet online), each graded and set out in an evidence-gap map (Table 4.3). Its policy conclusion is that, for ARFID, duties of design that act on recommender systems themselves reach further than rules about named categories of content. 5  Scribe, not judge: generative AI for early recognition and referral sets out a protocol in which a language model acts as a scribe rather than a judge: urgency is decided by fixed rules, observations are organised by dimension without scores, and a second model audits every draft. The chapter specifies an evaluation, with synthetic vignettes and pre-registered criteria, that should precede any claim that the protocol works. The interactive toolkit implements both the screening arithmetic of 1  Counting a moving target: context and prevalence and the prompt sequences of 5  Scribe, not judge: generative AI for early recognition and referral.
The Epilogue draws the argument together and makes recommendations for research, practice and governance. A bilingual page for anyone who is worried offers practical guidance and verified sources of help, and a bilingual Glossary, designed as a teaching resource for specialised translation, sets out the English and Spanish terminology.

title: Introduction
text:
Method and standards of evidence
This is a critical, evidence-graded synthesis, not a systematic review. Sources were identified through targeted, structured searches, mainly in PubMed, and through a curated corpus of studies and grey literature on social media, AI and eating disorders assembled for an earlier project. Bibliographic metadata for indexed articles were generated programmatically from PubMed records rather than typed by hand, and no reference entered the bibliography until its identifier had been checked. Reports by advocacy organisations, journalism and disclosed company documents are used where peer-reviewed evidence is absent, but they are identified as such and appraised in the text. Searches whose results are reported quantitatively are dated and their strings given (Table 1); the verification log, included in the archived release, records the rest.

Claims about the evidence carry a grade where it is thin or contested: E1 for systematic or meta-analytic evidence, E2 for several consistent primary studies, E3 for single studies, case reports or cross-sectional associations, and H for hypotheses with mechanistic plausibility only. The grades describe the support for a specific claim, not the quality of a source in general; a strong meta-analysis can support only a weak claim about ARFID. Every figure gives its source; simulations are labelled as such, their parameters are stated and their code can be inspected; numbers quoted from simulations are computed when the book is rendered.
The book follows safe-communication rules throughout: it gives no figures for weight, calories or portions, contains no images of bodies, and describes no behaviours in a way that could serve as instructions.
The limits of this method should be clear. Searches centred on PubMed will under-represent work indexed only in psychological, educational or computing databases and in Spanish-language bibliographic sources; the latter is a known gap that further work will address. The author writes from the philosophy of technology and the study of science, technology and society, not from clinical practice: clinical statements rest on the cited evidence, and the toolkit has not yet been evaluated with the people it is meant to serve. The book should be read as an argument that can be checked, and corrected, at each step.

crumbs: Introduction

title: 1  Counting a moving target: context and prevalence
text:
1.1 A diagnosis born in 2013
Epidemiology begins with a deceptively simple question: how many? For most psychiatric conditions the answer is contested at the margins but stable in its order of magnitude. For avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) it is not. Read naively, the literature suggests that ARFID affects roughly three in a thousand people, or one in fifty children, or one in ten of those sampled in pooled analyses, or one in four adults. A reader encountering these figures side by side might conclude that the field simply does not know. This chapter argues for a more useful conclusion: the figures differ because they measure different things, and the differences are themselves informative.
Three features make ARFID a moving target. The first is its youth as a diagnostic category. It entered the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders in 2013 and the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases later still, so the instruments for detecting it are new and the clinical populations used to calibrate them are small. The second is its internal heterogeneity: a single label covers a child who cannot tolerate the texture of most foods, an adolescent who rarely feels hungry, and a young person who stopped eating solid food after a frightening episode of choking. The third, and the one that most concerns this book, is that ARFID is defined partly by what it is not. Its criteria exclude any disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). A condition defined by an absence is hard to count with instruments designed to detect a presence.
The chapter proceeds in five steps. Section 1.1 traces how the diagnosis came to exist and how it is measured. Section 1.2 reviews the main estimates of frequency through four different lenses (clinical caseloads, surveillance of new cases, population and community studies, and pooled analyses) and explains why they diverge. Section 1.3 examines who is counted, by age, sex and co-occurring conditions. Section 1.4 addresses the distance between a positive screen and a confirmed diagnosis, which is the single most important epidemiological fact for anyone building an early-detection tool. Section 1.5 summarises what is known about the consequences of the disorder, and Section 1.6 sets out what the numbers cannot yet tell us.

title: 1  Counting a moving target: context and prevalence
text:
From a disorder of infancy to a disorder of the lifespan
Before 2013, children who ate too little or too narrowly, without the weight and shape concerns of anorexia nervosa, were classified either under feeding disorder of infancy or early childhood or under residual categories. The former required onset before the age of six (American Psychiatric Association, 2000), and so offered no home to an older child, an adolescent or an adult whose eating had become dangerously restricted for reasons unrelated to body image. Clinicians in adolescent medicine had long recognised such patients; what they lacked was a category that would let them be counted, studied and treated as a group.
The fifth edition of the DSM addressed the gap by replacing the infancy-bound diagnosis with ARFID and removing the age limit (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). In outline, the criteria require four things. First, an eating or feeding disturbance, such as an apparent lack of interest in eating, avoidance based on the sensory characteristics of food, or concern about the aversive consequences of eating, that results in a persistent failure to meet nutritional or energy needs. That failure must show itself in at least one of four ways: significant weight loss (or, in children, failure to achieve expected weight gain or faltering growth); significant nutritional deficiency; dependence on enteral feeding or oral nutritional supplements; or marked interference with psychosocial functioning. Second, the disturbance must not be better explained by a lack of available food or by a culturally sanctioned practice. Third, it must not occur exclusively during anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, and there must be no evidence of a disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced. Fourth, it must not be attributable to a concurrent medical condition or better explained by another mental disorder; where it occurs alongside such a condition, its severity must exceed what that condition would ordinarily produce.
The eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases, in force since January 2022, followed the same path. It places avoidant-restrictive food intake disorder (code 6B83) alongside anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge-eating disorder in a single grouping of feeding or eating disorders, and its description likewise excludes restriction explained by the unavailability of food, by another medical or mental condition, or by the effects of a substance (World Health Organization, 2025).
Two features of this definition shape everything that follows. The third criterion builds a body-image exclusion into the diagnosis itself, which is why the dominant public account of young people’s eating difficulties (the one that runs from appearance ideals through social comparison to restriction) does not describe ARFID (Dane & Bhatia, 2023). And the first criterion defines the disorder by its consequences (weight, growth, nutrition, supplements, functioning) as much as by its behaviours, which means that whether someone counts as a case depends heavily on whether those consequences are measured, and how.


Three presentations, one category
The DSM criteria name three illustrative drivers of restriction: sensory-based avoidance, lack of interest in eating or food, and fear of aversive consequences such as choking, vomiting or pain. Early instrument development treated these as three dimensions that can co-occur rather than as mutually exclusive subtypes (Bryant-Waugh et al., 2022; Zickgraf & Ellis, 2018). Empirical work has since confirmed that the boundaries are porous.
Two national surveillance studies have applied latent class analysis to children and adolescents newly diagnosed with ARFID. In Canada, a three-class model fitted best, with classes labelled acute medical, lack of appetite and sensory, to which cases were assigned with probabilities of 52%, 40.7% and 6.9% respectively. The acute-medical class was marked by recent weight loss, short illness duration and frequent hospitalisation; the lack-of-appetite class by failure to gain weight and faltering growth (Katzman et al., 2022). In the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland, four classes emerged, and the most common of them, accounting for 38.2% of cases, was a mixed presentation; the other three resembled the subtypes described in the literature. Age, sex, weight loss, distress around eating and an autism diagnosis predicted class membership (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Croudace, et al., 2024). A French study of parent reports reached a similar conclusion by a different route, identifying five profiles of which three were combinations (Rubio & Rigal, 2026).
The epidemiological consequence is easy to state and easy to forget: a single prevalence figure for ARFID aggregates groups that differ in age of onset, medical acuity, comorbidity and, plausibly, in the environmental factors that matter to them. When later chapters ask how environments shape the disorder, they will need to ask which presentation is at issue.


Measuring ARFID
Counting a disorder requires instruments, and ARFID’s instruments are young. Table 1.1 summarises those most often used in the studies discussed in this chapter. They fall into two families. Structured clinical interviews, such as the Pica, ARFID and Rumination Disorder Interview (PARDI), approximate a diagnostic assessment but are costly and require trained interviewers. Self-report and parent-report questionnaires, such as the Nine Item ARFID Screen (NIAS) and the PARDI-ARFID Questionnaire (PARDI-AR-Q), are cheap and scalable but measure symptoms, not diagnoses.



Table 1.1: Instruments most often used to detect or measure ARFID in the studies reviewed in this chapter.

Two observations from the table matter for the rest of the book. First, the validation samples are small and, for adolescents, recent. Second, the Spanish-language evidence is thin: a Mexican adaptation of the NIAS for youth, and its use in a specific adult clinical population in Spain. There is, as far as the searches for this chapter could establish, no validated instrument studied in a general population of Spanish adolescents. For a book whose toolkit offers prompts in Spanish, that is a gap to be acknowledged rather than papered over.






NoteA note on the Spanish name

The book will adopt the form used in the official Spanish edition of the relevant classification and record the choice in the Glossary.

section: 1.2 How common is ARFID? Four lenses
text:
1.2 How common is ARFID? Four lenses
The estimates of ARFID’s frequency are best read not as competing answers to one question but as answers to four different questions, each asked through a different lens. Table 1.2 summarises them; Figure 1.1 plots the prevalence estimates on a common scale.



Table 1.2: Four lenses on the frequency of ARFID. Estimates are not directly comparable: they differ in population, measure (share, incidence, prevalence), instrument and time window.











Lens
What is counted
Typical source
Illustrative estimates




Clinical caseload
Share of patients in specialist services who meet ARFID criteria
Retrospective chart reviews
5% of adolescent eating-disorder patients (Norris et al., 2014); 13.8% across seven North American adolescent-medicine programmes (Fisher et al., 2014); 22.5% in a day-treatment programme for younger patients (Nicely et al., 2014)


Surveillance of new cases

National paediatric and psychiatric surveillance units
2.02 per 100,000 aged 5–18 in Canada (Katzman et al., 2021); 2.79 per 100,000 aged 5–17 in the UK (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Lynn, et al., 2024)

Household surveys, school samples, linked registers, online panels

Pooled analysis

Systematic review and meta-analysis
11.14% (random effects) versus 4.51% (quality effects) (Nicholls-Clow et al., 2024)







Lens one: the clinical caseload
The first studies of ARFID were retrospective reviews of patients already in treatment. In a Canadian adolescent eating-disorder programme reviewing referrals between 2000 and 2011, 5% of patients met the new criteria (Norris et al., 2014). Across seven adolescent-medicine eating-disorder programmes in North America in 2010, 98 of 712 patients aged 8–18, or 13.8%, did so (Fisher et al., 2014). In a day-treatment programme for younger patients aged 7–17, the figure was 39 of 173, or 22.5% (Nicely et al., 2014). A systematic review later summarised the range in specialised eating-disorder services as 5–22.5%, and in specialist feeding clinics as 32–64% (Sanchez-Cerezo et al., 2023).
These figures say more about referral pathways than about populations. A day programme for younger children will see more ARFID than an adolescent programme designed around anorexia nervosa; a feeding clinic will see more still. The caseload lens is indispensable for planning services, but it cannot tell us how many young people in a community have the disorder, because it only sees those who arrive.


Lens two: surveillance of new cases
National surveillance systems ask a large panel of clinicians to report every new case they diagnose over a fixed period. Canada’s Paediatric Surveillance Program did this for ARFID in 2016–2017, surveying some 2,700 paediatricians monthly. It identified 207 new cases, with a mean age of 13.1 years, and estimated an incidence of 2.02 per 100,000 children and adolescents aged 5–18 (Katzman et al., 2021). A comparable study through the British Paediatric Surveillance Unit and the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Surveillance System, in 2021–2022, identified 319 eligible new cases aged 5–17, with a mean age of 11.2 years, and an observed annual incidence of 2.79 per 100,000 in the United Kingdom (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Lynn, et al., 2024).
These are rigorous studies, and their authors are explicit about what they measure: new cases that reach secondary care and are recognised as ARFID by a specialist. Everything upstream of that point (cases that are never referred, referred under another label, or managed in primary care) is invisible to the method. Surveillance therefore provides a floor, and a valuable one for service planning, but not an estimate of how many young people are affected.


Lens three: population and community studies
Population studies try to count cases where they live rather than where they are treated. They differ widely in method. Two sequential Australian household surveys of people aged over 15, conducted by interview in 2014 and 2015, found a three-month prevalence of ARFID of 0.3% in each year, lower than that of bulimia nervosa or broadly defined binge-eating disorder but associated with particularly poor mental health-related quality of life (Hay et al., 2017). A Swedish study linking parent reports from a national twin cohort to patient and prescription registers identified a broad ARFID phenotype in 682 of 33,902 children aged 6–12, or 2.0% (Dinkler et al., 2023). Across non-clinical samples of children and adolescents more generally, estimates have ranged from 0.3% to 15.5% (Sanchez-Cerezo et al., 2023).
At the far end of the range sits a population-based internet survey of 4,002 adults in the United Kingdom and the United States, with demographic quotas. Here 26.0% screened positive on the NIAS. Positive screens were more frequent among women than men (29.6% versus 22.1%) and declined with age, from 31.6% among those aged 18–39 to 16.1% among those aged 65 and over (Brownlow et al., 2026). The same dataset showed that positive screens were markedly more common among adults with disorders of gut–brain interaction, 34.6% against 19.4% among those without (Flack et al., 2026).


Lens four: pooling the evidence
The most comprehensive synthesis to date is a pre-registered meta-analysis of 26 studies published between 2013 and 2024, with a combined sample of 122,861 people (Nicholls-Clow et al., 2024). Its central finding is methodological. A conventional random-effects model gave a pooled prevalence of 11.14% (95% CI 8.16–14.5%). A quality-effects model, which weights studies by an appraisal of their methodological validity, gave 4.51% (95% CI 0.7–10.68%). Similar contrasts appeared in subgroups by gender, age group and clinical status. The authors draw two conclusions: that even the conservative estimate makes ARFID a common disorder, and that future studies need larger samples, standardised diagnostic measures and clearer reporting.








Figure 1.1: Reported frequency of ARFID by lens and setting. Points show single estimates; horizontal bars show confidence intervals or ranges across studies. The horizontal axis is logarithmic. Estimates differ in population, instrument, time window and definition, and are not directly comparable.







Reading the spread: the coastline problem
Set side by side, the prevalence estimates alone span two orders of magnitude, from three per thousand in an interview-based household survey to one in four positive screens in an online panel; incidence in specialist care, a different quantity, is lower still, at two to three new cases per 100,000 a year. It would be a mistake to average these figures, and an equal mistake to dismiss them.
A helpful analogy comes from geography. The length of a coastline depends on the length of the ruler used to measure it: a ruler a kilometre long skips every cove and headland, while a ruler a metre long follows each one, and the measured coastline grows accordingly. No measurement is wrong; each answers a question set by its instrument. The epidemiology of ARFID behaves similarly. A surveillance system that counts only specialist diagnoses uses a long ruler; a nine-item online screen uses a very short one, which follows every irregularity of eating, including many that would not meet diagnostic criteria. Between them, interview-based surveys and register linkage use rulers of intermediate length.
Three practical lessons follow. The first is that every figure should be quoted with its ruler attached: who was counted, how, where and over what period. The second is that the quality of the measurement matters at least as much as the size of the sample, as the contrast between the random-effects and quality-effects estimates shows (Nicholls-Clow et al., 2024). The third, developed in Section 1.4, is that the shorter the ruler, the more of what it detects will turn out, on closer inspection, not to be the disorder at all.
The broader context also deserves a word. Long-run epidemiological series from the Netherlands suggest that the overall incidence of eating disorders did not rise between 1975 and 2024, with the notable exception of anorexia nervosa among girls aged 10–14, while reported cases have risen in many countries since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic (Hoek, 2025). The rapid growth of ARFID in the clinical and research literature over the past decade should therefore be read, at least in part, as the visibility effect of a new category and of new instruments; none of the studies reviewed here measures a change in its incidence over time.

section: 1.3 Who is counted: age, sex and co-occurring conditions
text:
1.3 Who is counted: age, sex and co-occurring conditions

Age
Across clinical studies, young people with ARFID present earlier than those with anorexia nervosa. In the North American multi-site study, their mean age was 12.9 years against 15.6 for anorexia nervosa and 16.5 for bulimia nervosa, and they had been unwell for longer before presenting: 33.3 months on average, against 14.5 and 23.5 (Fisher et al., 2014). In a Spanish clinical sample from the Hospital Sant Joan de Déu in Barcelona, patients with ARFID were younger at assessment (10.8 against 14.1 years), had an earlier onset (6.2 against 13.4 years) and a much longer course before assessment (61.2 against 8.4 months) than those with anorexia nervosa (Cañas et al., 2021). Onset is commonly before puberty, which makes growth a key marker of impact (Tanner & Richmond, 2024).
Age also shapes the presentation. In the Canadian surveillance data, older children and adolescents were more likely than younger children to report eating too little and loss of appetite, to be medically compromised, to have co-occurring anxiety and depression, and to be admitted to hospital: 13.3% of those aged 5–9, 41.7% of those aged 10–14 and 55.6% of those aged 15–18 (Katzman et al., 2021). For an adolescent-focused book, this is a sobering gradient: the age band on which the toolkit concentrates is also the one in which ARFID is most likely to be medically serious by the time it is recognised.


Sex
ARFID’s sex distribution differs from that of anorexia nervosa, but not in a single direction across settings. In clinical samples, boys make up a markedly larger share of ARFID than of anorexia nervosa: 29% against 15% in the North American multi-site study (Fisher et al., 2014), and 60.6% against 6.1% in the Spanish sample (Cañas et al., 2021); earlier Canadian and US studies reported the same tendency (Nicely et al., 2014; Norris et al., 2014). UK surveillance found a slightly higher incidence in boys than in girls (2.98 against 2.58 per 100,000) (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Lynn, et al., 2024), whereas in the Canadian surveillance sample 61.4% of cases were girls (Katzman et al., 2021). Among adults screened online, positive screens were more common in women (Brownlow et al., 2026).
The inconsistency is itself a finding. It suggests that the sex ratio depends on age, on referral pathways and on the instrument, and it warns against importing assumptions from anorexia nervosa, whose overwhelmingly female profile has shaped both public images of eating disorders and, potentially, the training data of the AI systems discussed in Chapter 5.


Co-occurring conditions
Co-occurring conditions are the rule rather than the exception. A systematic review of child and adolescent studies reported anxiety disorders in 9.1–72% of cases and autism in 8.2–54.75% (Sanchez-Cerezo et al., 2023); a later meta-analysis estimated that 16.27% of people with ARFID have an autism diagnosis (Sader et al., 2025). In the North American multi-site study, 55% of patients with ARFID had a co-occurring medical condition, against 10% of those with anorexia nervosa, and 58% had an anxiety disorder, while mood disorders were less frequent (19% against 31%) (Fisher et al., 2014). In the Spanish sample, medical comorbidity was found in 42.4% of patients with ARFID against 12.1% of those with anorexia nervosa, and psychiatric comorbidity in 81.8% against 33.3% (Cañas et al., 2021). Youth with ARFID in a US study were more than ten times as likely as healthy controls to report gastrointestinal conditions (37% against 3%) and twice as likely to report immune-mediated conditions (Burton-Murray et al., 2024).
These patterns matter for counting in two ways. They concentrate risk in identifiable groups (autistic young people, those with anxiety, those with gastrointestinal and immune conditions), which is where targeted screening is most efficient (Section 2.4). And they complicate the fourth diagnostic criterion: when a young person with a digestive condition restricts food, the clinician must judge whether the restriction exceeds what the condition would ordinarily produce. A study of adults with systemic sclerosis in Spain, in which 49.5% screened positive on the Spanish NIAS, just over half of them on the fear-of-consequences dimension, illustrates how hard that judgement can be (Alcala-Gonzalez et al., 2025).

title: 1  Counting a moving target: context and prevalence
text:
1.4 From positive screen to diagnosis

The base-rate problem
The figure of 26% positive screens among adults (Brownlow et al., 2026) is not a prevalence of ARFID, and its authors do not present it as one. The distance between a positive screen and a confirmed diagnosis is the single most important epidemiological fact for the design of early-detection tools, and it can be measured.
In a validation study drawn from a large genetic study of ARFID, 25 adults and 25 parents of children who had screened positive were assessed with the PARDI interview. The proportion of screen-positives confirmed as ARFID, the positive predictive value (PPV), was 55.0% for adults and 76.0% for parent reports with the PARDI-AR-Q, and 45.8% and 64.0% with the NIAS (Ortiz et al., 2025). Even in a sample recruited into a study of ARFID, whose members had already screened positive, between about a quarter and just over half of positive screens did not correspond to a diagnosis.
In the general population the proportion would be lower, for a reason that has nothing to do with the quality of any particular questionnaire. The PPV of a test depends not only on its sensitivity (the share of true cases it detects) and specificity (the share of non-cases it correctly clears) but also on the prevalence of the condition in the group tested. When a condition is uncommon, even a good test produces more false alarms than true detections, because the false alarms are drawn from the much larger pool of people without the condition.
A worked example makes the point concrete. Imagine a screen with 85% sensitivity and 85% specificity, figures chosen for illustration rather than taken from any instrument, applied to 1,000 adolescents. If the true prevalence is 4.5%, close to the quality-effects estimate, about 45 of them have ARFID; the screen detects 38 and misses 7. Of the 955 without ARFID, 15% (about 143) also screen positive. Of the 181 positive screens, then, only 38, or roughly one in five, are true cases. If the true prevalence is 11.1%, close to the random-effects estimate, the PPV rises to about 41%: better, but still a minority. Figure 1.2 shows how the PPV changes across the plausible range of prevalence for four combinations of sensitivity and specificity; the toolkit lets readers explore the same calculation interactively.








Figure 1.2: Positive predictive value of a screen as a function of the prevalence of ARFID in the screened group, for four illustrative combinations of sensitivity and specificity (not those of any specific instrument). Dashed lines mark the pooled prevalence estimates from quality-effects (4.51%) and random-effects (11.14%) models.







An alarm needs an officer
Airport security offers a familiar analogy. The walk-through metal detector is deliberately sensitive: it sounds for belt buckles, keys and coins far more often than for anything dangerous, and nobody regards this as a failure. It works because a second, more specific step follows: an officer with a hand-held detector who resolves each alarm. A screening questionnaire is the arch; a clinical assessment is the officer. A screen deployed without a clear route to assessment is an alarm without an officer: it produces anxiety, labels and, in a young population, a real risk of iatrogenic harm, without the means of resolving any of it.






ImportantFor practice




A positive screen for ARFID is a reason for a conversation and a referral, not a diagnosis. In community settings, most positive screens will not be confirmed.
Where screening is used, it should be targeted at groups with higher prior probability (for example autistic young people, or those attending gastroenterology or anxiety services), where the PPV is higher (Section 2.4).
Signs of medical compromise (weight loss, faltering growth, dependence on supplements, or physiological instability) warrant medical assessment irrespective of any questionnaire score.



This is the epidemiological foundation of the design principles set out in Section 5.4. A tool aimed at worried parents, teachers or young people will, by construction, be used in groups where most people do not have the disorder. If such a tool labelled, most of its labels would be wrong. It must therefore route rather than label: organise observations, signal urgency where present, and hand the decision to a professional.

title: 1  Counting a moving target: context and prevalence
text:
1.5 Burden and consequences
If ARFID’s frequency is uncertain, its seriousness in clinical populations is not. Young people with ARFID in clinical series are frequently underweight: in the North American multi-site study, their median body weight was intermediate between that of patients with anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa (Fisher et al., 2014), and a day-treatment cohort showed degrees of weight loss and malnutrition similar to those of other eating disorders, together with greater dependence on nutritional supplements (Nicely et al., 2014). In a Canadian adolescent programme, about a third of patients with ARFID required hospital admission for medical instability, and four of 34 were later reclassified as having anorexia nervosa as their symptoms evolved (Norris et al., 2014). Because onset often precedes puberty, faltering growth and its long-term consequences for adult height require monitoring against genetic potential (Tanner & Richmond, 2024). Nutritional restriction may also leave metabolic traces: youth with ARFID showed elevated triglycerides and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein more often than healthy controls, which the authors relate to limited dietary variety (Burton-Murray et al., 2024).
The burden extends beyond the medical. In the Australian household surveys, people with ARFID had poor mental health-related quality of life and lower role performance than people without an eating disorder (Hay et al., 2017). Among adults screened online, a positive ARFID screen was associated with underweight, somatic symptoms, mood disturbance, reduced physical and mental quality of life and greater use of healthcare (Brownlow et al., 2026). Qualitative work with adult women describes the disorder’s lived texture as a trade-off between safety and freedom: restriction protects against the unknowns of food at the cost of spontaneity and social life (Ruiz Fischer & Starr, 2024).
On outcomes, the evidence is thinner. At one-year follow-up in UK surveillance, clinicians judged that 54.8% of cases had improved (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Lynn, et al., 2024), a figure that is encouraging but rests on clinical impression rather than standardised measures. Systematic evidence on psychological treatment for ARFID remains scarce compared with other eating disorders (Russell et al., 2023), and difficulties linked to sensory sensitivity and mealtime routines often persist into adolescence and adulthood, particularly among autistic people (Keski-Rahkonen & Ruusunen, 2023). We have not located population-based mortality estimates for ARFID; the long-run mortality literature on eating disorders largely predates the category.

section: 1.6 What the numbers cannot tell us
text:
1.6 What the numbers cannot tell us
Four limits deserve to be stated plainly, because each shapes what the rest of this book can and cannot claim.
Heterogeneity of method. The studies reviewed here differ in population, setting, instrument, threshold and time window, and they are dominated by English-speaking countries and by retrospective clinical data (Nicholls-Clow et al., 2024; Sanchez-Cerezo et al., 2023). Any single figure is a coordinate in this space, not a fact about ARFID as such.
What surveillance cannot see. Incidence studies count what reaches specialists. In systems where primary care and schools are the first point of contact, much of the disorder’s natural history unfolds before, or without, specialist recognition. The gap between incidence in secondary care and prevalence in the community is precisely the space in which early detection operates.
Spain and Spanish-speaking adolescents. The evidence available for Spain is limited to a paediatric clinical sample (Cañas et al., 2021) and to adults with a specific medical condition (Alcala-Gonzalez et al., 2025). In the searches conducted for this chapter we found no population-based estimates for Spanish children or adolescents, and no screening instrument validated in that population; the closest is a Spanish-language adaptation validated in Mexican youth (Medina-Tepal et al., 2023). Awareness of ARFID among adolescents themselves is reported to be limited, although the available data are sparse (Zięba et al., 2025).


Where else to look. Spanish-language evidence may sit outside PubMed. Readers extending this search could try IBECS (the Spanish health-sciences index of the Instituto de Salud Carlos III) and Dialnet, with strings such as ARFID, TERIA, «evitación/restricción de la ingesta» or «alimentación selectiva» AND (infancia OR adolescencia), and the eating-disorder programme reports and activity data published by the regional health services.
The body-image boundary. The exclusion of weight and shape concern is clear on paper but porous in practice. Young people grow up surrounded by appearance ideals, and a child with ARFID may also value thinness without that value driving the restriction (Barney et al., 2022); conversely, some patients first classified as ARFID later meet criteria for anorexia nervosa (Norris et al., 2014). Instruments that measure the two families of motivation separately (Çelik et al., 2026) are necessary, but the boundary will remain a site of clinical judgement.
These limits point forward. Chapter 2 takes up the heterogeneity of presentations and the groups at highest risk. Chapter 3 asks how genetic liability and environments combine. Chapter 4 asks what digital environments might add, a question that, as this chapter has shown, cannot be answered without first being clear about what is being counted. And Chapter 5 draws the practical conclusion of Section 1.4: in groups where most people do not have the disorder, a responsible tool routes, and does not label.






NoteKey points




ARFID entered the DSM in 2013 and ICD-11 as code 6B83; it is defined partly by the absence of weight and shape concern, and by consequences for weight, growth, nutrition and functioning.
Its three classic presentations (sensory, lack of interest, fear) frequently combine; mixed presentations are common.
Frequency estimates span two orders of magnitude because they measure different things: clinical caseload, incidence in specialist care, population prevalence, positive screens, and pooled averages.
The quality of the measurement changes the answer: pooled prevalence falls from 11.14% to 4.51% when studies are weighted by quality.
In community settings most positive screens are not confirmed; tools for the public must route to assessment rather than label.

title: 2  A family of difficulties: related disorders, ages and groups
text:
2.1 The feeding and eating disorders family
Chapter 1 showed that how often ARFID is found depends on how it is looked for. This chapter turns from how many to what and who: what kind of difficulty ARFID is, how it differs from its neighbours, and which young people are most likely to develop it. These questions are not merely taxonomic. Every argument about environmental causes in the chapters that follow presupposes that we know which presentation, in which group, at which age we are talking about. A mealtime practice, a medical condition or a stream of online content that matters for a frightened adolescent may be irrelevant to a child with lifelong sensory aversions.
The chapter proceeds in five steps. Section 2.1 situates ARFID within the family of feeding and eating disorders recognised by current classifications. Section 2.2 examines its three presentations and the evidence that they combine. Section 2.3 maps the borders with its look-alikes: picky eating, paediatric feeding disorder, anorexia nervosa, orthorexic eating and restriction secondary to medical illness. Section 2.4 identifies the groups in which ARFID is concentrated, and Section 2.5 follows the disorder across childhood, adolescence and adulthood.

title: 2  A family of difficulties: related disorders, ages and groups
text:
One grouping, two traditions
Both major classifications now place feeding disorders, historically the province of paediatrics, and eating disorders, historically that of adolescent and adult psychiatry, in a single grouping (American Psychiatric Association, 2022; World Health Organization, 2025). Table 2.1 summarises its members. The grouping is pragmatic rather than theoretical: what its members share is a disturbance of eating that harms health or functioning, not a common cause.



Table 2.1: The feeding and eating disorders grouping in current classifications. Core features are paraphrased; consult the classifications for the full criteria. Sources: American Psychiatric Association (2022); World Health Organization (2025); Dane and Bhatia (2023).











Disorder
Core feature (paraphrased)
Role of weight and shape concern
ICD-11




Anorexia nervosa
Restriction leading to significantly low body weight, with intense fear of weight gain or behaviour that prevents it

6B80

Recurrent binge eating with compensatory behaviours such as purging

6B81

A useful way to read the table is through Wittgenstein’s notion of family resemblance: members related by a network of overlapping similarities rather than by one feature that all of them share. Anorexia nervosa and ARFID share restriction, low weight and medical risk; ARFID and binge-eating disorder share the absence of a required body-image criterion; anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa share the overvaluation of weight and shape. No single feature, and certainly not body image, defines the family.


The residual categories are large
A recurring finding in population studies is that the “other” and “unspecified” categories are larger than the named disorders. In the Australian household surveys discussed in Section 1.2.3, the three-month prevalence of other specified feeding or eating disorders was 3.2% and that of unspecified disorders 10.4%, against 0.3% for ARFID and 0.4–0.5% for broadly defined anorexia nervosa (Hay et al., 2017). In a German sample of 82 patients aged 0–17 seeking treatment for restrictive eating, the move from ICD-10 to ICD-11 significantly reduced the number of residual diagnoses, as patients crossed over to full-threshold anorexia nervosa or ARFID. Those reclassified as ARFID were younger, had an earlier onset and more restrictive eating behaviours, and tended to have more somatic comorbidity than those reclassified as anorexia nervosa (Düplois et al., 2023).
The point matters for a book about early recognition. Before ARFID existed as a category, many of the young people now diagnosed with it were held in residual categories that carried little clinical guidance and attracted little research. Part of what ARFID has done is to give a name, and therefore a research agenda, to a group that was always there.

title: 2  A family of difficulties: related disorders, ages and groups
text:
2.2 Three presentations, many combinations

Three dials rather than three boxes
The diagnostic criteria name three drivers of restriction (sensory-based avoidance, lack of interest in eating or food, and fear of aversive consequences), and early work proposed that each reflects a distinct neurobiological system: sensory perception, homeostatic appetite and the negative-valence (threat) systems respectively (Thomas et al., 2017). The same authors argued for a dimensional rather than categorical reading: each young person sits somewhere on each of the three dimensions. The image is of three dials, each of which can be turned up or down, rather than three boxes into which patients must be sorted. Table 2.2 summarises what is known about each dimension.



Table 2.2: The three ARFID presentations. Mixed presentations, most often combining sensory avoidance and lack of interest, are common.












Presentation
What drives restriction
Typical onset and course
Weight and medical profile
Frequently associated features




Sensory-based avoidance
Taste, smell, texture, colour or appearance of food; rigid rules (specific brands, foods that must not touch)
Often long-standing, from early childhood; more persistent (Kambanis et al., 2025)
Occurs across the weight spectrum; narrow variety can affect nutrition (Burton-Murray et al., 2024)
More often co-occurs with autism (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Croudace, et al., 2024)


Lack of interest in eating or food
Low appetite, early fullness, little pleasure or interest in eating
Long-standing; more persistent (Kambanis et al., 2025)
Underweight, failure to gain weight, faltering growth (Katzman et al., 2022)
Combines frequently with sensory avoidance


Fear of aversive consequences
Fear of choking, vomiting, pain or allergic reaction, often after a specific episode
Often acute onset; more likely to remit by two years (Kambanis et al., 2025)
Underweight, recent weight loss (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Croudace, et al., 2024)
Anxiety in most cases; girls over-represented (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Croudace, et al., 2024)








What the data show
Three lines of evidence support the dimensional view. The first comes from latent class analyses of national surveillance samples, introduced in Section 1.1.2. In the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland, an analysis based on six indicators of ARFID psychopathology (lack of appetite, lack of interest, difficulties with the practicalities of eating, sensory sensitivity, rigid eating and fear of aversive consequences) found that the most common class, at 38.2% of 319 children and adolescents, was a mixed presentation combining sensory sensitivity and lack of interest. The remaining cases divided between a sensory class, a lack-of-appetite class and, least commonly at 7.2%, a fear class (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Croudace, et al., 2024). The classes differed in revealing ways. Membership of the mixed class was associated with younger age, male sex, distress around eating and an autism diagnosis. The fear class was distinctive: almost 80% were girls, most were underweight with an acute onset, and more than 80% had co-occurring anxiety. The authors suggest that, within an otherwise dimensional disorder, fear-driven ARFID may be a relatively separate group. The Canadian analysis had earlier identified acute medical, lack of appetite and sensory classes, with a further 14.5% of cases sitting between the first two (Katzman et al., 2022; Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Croudace, et al., 2024).
The second line of evidence comes from community and clinical samples that measure the three dimensions directly. Among adults with disorders of gut–brain interaction, positive screens were driven by lack of interest in 21.5% of the sample, by sensory avoidance in 18.1% and by fear of aversive consequences in 9.9% (Flack et al., 2026), and a French study of parent reports identified five profiles, three of them combinations (Rubio & Rigal, 2026).
The third line of evidence is prognostic, and arguably the most important. In a prospective study of 100 young people aged 9–23 followed for two years with the PARDI interview, half still met criteria at the end of the follow-up. Greater severity on the sensory and lack-of-interest dimensions predicted persistence at one year, whereas greater severity on the fear dimension predicted remission at two years (Kambanis et al., 2025). If the dimensions predict course, they are not merely descriptive conveniences. They are also likely to matter for environmental questions: an acute, fear-driven presentation triggered by a frightening episode is a plausible candidate for environmental influences, digital ones included (Chapter 4), in a way that a lifelong sensory profile may not be.

text:
2.3 Boundaries and look-alikes
ARFID’s criteria are written partly in the negative: not explained by lack of food, by culture, by another eating disorder or by a medical condition. In practice, each of these exclusions marks a border that clinicians, teachers and parents must cross with care. Table 2.3 summarises the main look-alikes.



Table 2.3: Distinguishing ARFID from its look-alikes. The table is a guide to the questions that matter, not a diagnostic instrument.











Condition
What drives restriction
Weight or shape concern
Distinguishing questions




Picky eating and food neophobia
Reluctance to try new foods; preferences
Absent
Is growth, nutrition or daily life affected? Most children outgrow it (Pjetraj et al., 2025)


Paediatric feeding disorder

Picky eating, neophobia and paediatric feeding disorder
Picky eating is common: estimates range from 13% to 50% of children, with a peak between the ages of two and six, and most children outgrow it without harm. A minority, however, remain at risk of long-term nutritional compromise and psychosocial difficulty, and the factors that contribute to it (genetic predisposition, sensory sensitivity, temperament, family feeding practices and adverse feeding experiences) overlap substantially with those implicated in ARFID (Pjetraj et al., 2025). A systematic review of food neophobia, the reluctance to try new foods, identified parental pressure to eat, low encouragement at mealtimes, sensory aspects of food and childhood anxiety among associated factors (Torres et al., 2020).
The boundary between ordinary restriction and disorder is consequence, and a German study of general paediatric inpatients shows how much depends on drawing it carefully. Of 111 patients aged 8–18 in hospital for physical illnesses, 68% reported at least one restrictive eating behaviour. Only 7%, however, showed symptoms of ARFID once medical records were combined with self-report, particularly those who were underweight (Schöffel et al., 2021). Restriction is common; restriction with consequences is not.
A further neighbour is paediatric feeding disorder, a term proposed by a multidisciplinary consensus to describe impaired oral intake that is not appropriate for age and is associated with medical, nutritional, feeding-skill or psychosocial dysfunction (Goday et al., 2019). The two concepts grew largely out of different professional traditions (paediatric gastroenterology and feeding therapy on one side, psychiatry on the other), and they overlap in young children. For this book, the practical lesson is that a child whose restriction involves difficulties with chewing or swallowing, or a medical component, may need a feeding team as much as a mental-health service.


Anorexia nervosa and the motivational boundary
The defining contrast between ARFID and anorexia nervosa is motivational, and longitudinal studies support it. In an 18-month study of 82 young women aged 10–23 with low-weight eating disorders, ARFID was the most stable diagnosis (a probability of 0.84 of remaining in the same category), and no patient with another diagnosis crossed over into ARFID (Breithaupt et al., 2022). In the two-year study discussed above, 3% of young people with ARFID developed anorexia nervosa (Kambanis et al., 2025); in an earlier Canadian clinical series, four of 34 were reclassified as their symptoms evolved (Norris et al., 2014). Crossover from ARFID to anorexia nervosa is therefore uncommon but real, and it is one reason why a first assessment should not be treated as final.
The psychopathological profiles differ as well. In the Spanish clinical sample from Sant Joan de Déu, young people with ARFID showed more clinical fears and attention problems, while those with anorexia nervosa reported more internalising symptoms such as anxiety and depression on self-report questionnaires (Cañas et al., 2021). Yet the boundary remains porous at the level of individual experience: a child with ARFID can absorb appearance ideals from the culture around her without those ideals driving her restriction (Barney et al., 2022). Measures that separate the two families of motivation are necessary for exactly this reason (Çelik et al., 2026).


Orthorexic eating
Orthorexia nervosa, a pathological preoccupation with eating “correctly”, is not a recognised diagnosis. A Delphi consensus of 47 experts from 14 countries proposed provisional criteria, while acknowledging that empirical evidence is limited (Donini et al., 2022). A Japanese case illustrates why the concept matters for this book. A 13-year-old girl presented with rapid weight loss; she did not fear weight gain, which argued against anorexia nervosa, and she did not avoid foods for sensory or fear-based reasons, which argued against ARFID. Her restriction was driven instead by rules about nutrition that she had taken from magazines and social media promoting a diet based almost exclusively on vegetables (Yoshimura et al., 2023). A single case proves nothing about prevalence, but it marks a boundary at which digital information environments plausibly enter the clinical picture (Section 4.3).


Restriction in the context of medical illness
The fourth criterion requires that restriction exceed what a concurrent medical condition would ordinarily produce. This is a judgement, not a measurement. The investigators of the Spanish systemic sclerosis study, in which half of patients screened positive, concluded that future research must identify when a positive screen reflects an adaptive response to disease and when it reflects pathological restriction warranting behavioural treatment (Alcala-Gonzalez et al., 2025). The same question arises in every gastrointestinal and immune-mediated condition discussed in Section 2.4.
