title: 2  A family of difficulties: related disorders, ages and groups
text:
2.4 Groups at elevated risk
ARFID is not evenly distributed. It concentrates in identifiable groups, and those groups are where early recognition is most efficient: as Section 1.4 showed, a screen has a higher positive predictive value where prior probability is higher. Figure 2.1 brings together estimates from clinical populations; they use different measures and should be compared with caution.








Figure 2.1: Frequency of ARFID or of positive ARFID screens in selected clinical populations. Points show single estimates; the horizontal bar shows a 95% confidence interval. Colour distinguishes screening questionnaires from clinical criteria or diagnoses. Positive screens are not diagnoses, and estimates come from different countries, ages and instruments.






Neurodevelopmental conditions
The strongest and best-documented association is with autism. A meta-analysis of 21 studies and 7,442 participants estimated that 16.27% of people with ARFID have an autism diagnosis (95% CI 8.64–28.53%) and that 11.41% of autistic groups meet criteria or thresholds for ARFID (95% CI 2.89–35.76%), with gender and ethnicity as significant sources of heterogeneity (Sader et al., 2025). In a large autism cohort, avoidant-restrictive features were reported in 21% of participants and in 17% of their parents, and sensory sensitivities, food preferences and mealtime routines often persist into adolescence and adulthood (Keski-Rahkonen & Ruusunen, 2023). Demand for help is high: in a survey of 419 community feeding practitioners in the United States, 97% reported seeing autistic children with feeding problems, food selectivity was the most common presenting problem, and those who did not offer treatment most often cited insufficient training (Burrell et al., 2025).
Population data broaden the picture. In a Swedish cohort of 30,795 children, the 600 with an ARFID phenotype had elevated symptoms on every one of the neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions measured. The most prevalent were separation anxiety (29.0%), oppositional defiant disorder (19.4%), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD, 16.9%), panic disorder (15.3%) and tic disorders (14.8%); the largest increases in odds were for autism (odds ratio 13.7) and ADHD (9.4), with no sex-specific differences (Nyholmer et al., 2025). ADHD raises a specific clinical dilemma, because stimulant medication commonly suppresses appetite. A case series of ten young people treated for both conditions found that stimulants could be continued, with dose optimisation and structured mealtimes, while weight was restored (Finn et al., 2023), an encouraging but small-scale observation.


Anxiety and obsessive–compulsive symptoms
Anxiety is the most frequent psychiatric companion of ARFID in children and adolescents, with estimates ranging from 9.1% to 72% across studies (Sanchez-Cerezo et al., 2023); in the British surveillance data, more than 80% of the fear class had co-occurring anxiety (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Croudace, et al., 2024). The relationship with obsessive–compulsive disorder is partial: a systematic review found overlapping and distinct features, lower obsessive–compulsive comorbidity in childhood and adolescence than in adulthood, and an association in younger people between obsessive–compulsive disorder and the fear-driven profile. Obsessive–compulsive symptoms may respond poorly to conventional eating-disorder treatment (Di Luzio et al., 2026).


Gastrointestinal, immune and other medical conditions
The third major risk group comprises young people and adults with gastrointestinal, immune-mediated and other chronic conditions. Among adults attending gastroenterology clinics for disorders of gut–brain interaction, 39.8% reported ARFID symptoms, three times the proportion with clinically significant weight- or shape-motivated eating-disorder symptoms (Burton Murray et al., 2022). Similar patterns appear in population data (Flack et al., 2026), in coeliac disease and non-coeliac gluten sensitivity, where ARFID symptoms were found in 19% of patients at consultation and were associated with a history of weight loss (Atkins et al., 2026), in inflammatory bowel disease, where positive screens were associated with lower food literacy (Yin et al., 2023), and in cystic fibrosis (Kass et al., 2022). The association runs in both directions: youth with ARFID were more than ten times as likely as healthy controls to report gastrointestinal conditions and twice as likely to report immune-mediated conditions, which the authors interpret as suggesting bidirectional risk and maintenance factors (Burton-Murray et al., 2024).
For early recognition, these findings have a double edge. They identify clinics where screening is likely to be productive. But they also place the hardest judgement of all, whether restriction is adaptive or disordered (Section 2.3.4), in exactly the settings where the risk is highest.


Families
ARFID is lived in families. Parents of children with sensory sensitivities and picky eating describe a daily battle for control of the sensory environment, the stigma and disapproval of others, and a gradual movement towards acceptance that made positive interactions around food possible (Cunliffe et al., 2022). Among adolescents in treatment, family functioning was impaired and comparable to that of adolescents with restricting anorexia nervosa, although it was not associated with the severity of ARFID symptoms (Rienecke et al., 2026). Neither study can tell us whether family strain is a cause or a consequence; both tell us that families are part of the clinical picture, and part of any early-recognition strategy.






ImportantFor practice




When picky eating needs attention: when it is accompanied by weight loss, faltering growth, reliance on supplements or drinks in place of meals, or marked interference with school, friendships or family life.
Where to look first: autistic young people and those with ADHD; young people with anxiety, especially after a frightening episode of choking or vomiting; and those attending gastroenterology, allergy or other chronic-illness clinics.
What to ask: which driver (sensory, interest, fear, or weight and shape) and what consequences. A worry about weight or shape points towards a broad eating-disorder assessment, not away from help.

text:
2.5 Across the life course

Childhood
Restrictive eating has its first and most common expression in early childhood, when picky eating peaks (Pjetraj et al., 2025). ARFID onset is commonly before puberty (Tanner & Richmond, 2024), and population data place the broad phenotype at about 2% of children aged 6–12 (Dinkler et al., 2023). In clinical series, children with ARFID are younger and have been unwell for longer than those with anorexia nervosa when they first present (Cañas et al., 2021; Fisher et al., 2014). The mixed sensory and lack-of-interest presentation, associated with younger age and autism, is characteristic of this period (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Croudace, et al., 2024).


Adolescence
Adolescence, the focus of this book and of its toolkit, is the period in which ARFID changes character. A representative survey of 5,072 secondary-school students aged 11–19 in New South Wales found a prevalence of possible ARFID of 1.98% (95% CI 1.63–2.41%), similar to that of anorexia nervosa and binge-eating disorder in the same population and stable across school years. The ratio of boys to girls was 1:1.7, a statistically significant but small difference. Weight status, psychological distress and health-related quality of life did not differ between adolescents with and without possible ARFID, which led the authors to suggest that its impact may be modest in adolescence and become more significant in adulthood (Van Buuren et al., 2023). Clinical samples tell a different story: among Canadian children and adolescents reaching specialist care, older age was associated with eating too little, loss of appetite, medical compromise, anxiety and depression, and hospital admission (Katzman et al., 2021); in British surveillance data, the inability to eat with others and the avoidance of social activities involving food distinguished between presentations (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Croudace, et al., 2024).
The two pictures are compatible. A community survey captures many adolescents with milder, stable restriction who are getting by; specialist services see those in whom restriction has crossed into medical or social harm. Early recognition is about the passage between the two, and adolescence, when meals move out of the family home and into school canteens, friendships and independent choices, is where that passage is most likely to become visible.
Course is variable. Over two years, half of young people with ARFID in a prospective study persisted with the diagnosis (Kambanis et al., 2025). Over 18 months, ARFID was the most stable of the low-weight eating disorders (Breithaupt et al., 2022). In British surveillance data, clinicians judged that 54.8% of cases had improved at one year (Sanchez-Cerezo, Neale, Julius, Lynn, et al., 2024).


Adulthood
ARFID is not a disorder that young people simply grow out of. In adults, positive screens are common and associated with a substantial health burden (Brownlow et al., 2026), interview-based prevalence is low but associated with poor mental health-related quality of life (Hay et al., 2017), and adults describe living with the disorder as a trade-off between the safety of known foods and the freedom of ordinary social life (Ruiz Fischer & Starr, 2024). Among autistic people in particular, sensory and routine-based difficulties often continue into adulthood (Keski-Rahkonen & Ruusunen, 2023).

section: 2.6 Implications for the rest of the book
text:
2.6 Implications for the rest of the book
Three conclusions carry forward. First, ARFID is dimensional, and its dimensions predict course; analyses of environmental influence in Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 must therefore ask which dimension is affected, not only whether ARFID is. Second, risk is concentrated in identifiable groups (neurodevelopmental, anxious, and medically ill young people), which is where targeted recognition is most efficient and where the toolkit’s risk-context modules (Section 5.5) are directed. Third, the borders with picky eating, paediatric feeding disorder, anorexia nervosa, orthorexic eating and medical illness are crossed by judgement, not by measurement. A responsible tool can help adults describe what they see along each of these borders; it cannot, and should not, decide on which side a young person stands.






NoteKey points




Feeding and eating disorders form a single grouping held together by family resemblance, not by a shared cause; body image defines some members and is explicitly excluded from ARFID.
ARFID’s three presentations (sensory, lack of interest, fear) behave like dimensions: mixed presentations are the most common in children, and the dimensions predict course, with fear-driven ARFID more acute and more likely to remit.
Restriction is common; restriction with nutritional, medical or psychosocial consequences is not. Consequences mark the border with picky eating.
Crossover from ARFID to anorexia nervosa is uncommon but real; motivations should be reassessed over time.
Risk concentrates in autistic young people and those with ADHD, in anxious young people, and in those with gastrointestinal, immune and other chronic conditions.

2  A family of difficulties: related disorders, ages and groups

title: 3  Seed and soil: genetic and environmental determinants
text:
3.1 What heritability does and does not mean
The title of this book promises an account of the environmental factors in feeding and eating disorders. The most robust single finding about the causes of ARFID seems, at first sight, to undercut that promise: in the largest twin study to date, about four-fifths of the variation in liability to ARFID was attributable to genetic differences (Dinkler et al., 2023). A reader might reasonably ask what is left for the environment to explain.
This chapter argues that the question rests on a misunderstanding, and that clearing it up is the most useful thing a book about environments can do. Heritability is a statement about the sources of variation in a population under a given range of conditions. It is not a statement about how much of any one child’s difficulty is “in the genes”, and it says nothing about whether changing the environment would change the outcome. The gardener’s image captures the point: the seed shapes what kind of plant can grow, but soil, water and weather decide whether, when and how it does, and a gardener who knows that most of the variation in a field is due to seed has learnt nothing about what to do for one plant.
The chapter proceeds in eight steps. Section 3.1 explains what twin studies of ARFID and related traits have found and what they cannot show. Section 3.2 turns to molecular genetics. Section 3.3, Section 3.4, Section 3.5 and Section 3.6 examine four layers of environment for which there is evidence: the developmental, the familial, the bodily and the social. Section 3.7 asks what treatment trials reveal about environmental levers, and Section 3.8 draws the evidence together in a working model that prepares the ground for the discussion of digital environments in Chapter 4.

title: 3  Seed and soil: genetic and environmental determinants
text:
What twin studies estimate
Twin studies compare identical twins, who share all their genes, with non-identical twins, who share on average half of the genetic variants that differ between people. If identical twins resemble each other more closely than non-identical twins, the excess similarity is attributed to genes. The variation in a trait is then partitioned into three components: additive genetic influences (A, whose share is the heritability), environmental influences shared by siblings growing up in the same family (C) and environmental influences unique to each individual (E), a component that also absorbs measurement error.
The Swedish twin study introduced in Chapter 1 applied this design to 16,951 twin pairs. Drawing on parent reports at ages 9 or 12 together with patient and prescription registers, it identified a broad ARFID phenotype in 2.0% of children aged 6–12. The heritability of ARFID was 0.79 (95% CI 0.70–0.85), and the remaining variation was attributed to non-shared environmental factors (0.21; 95% CI 0.15–0.30). The estimates barely changed when children with autism or with medical illnesses that could account for the restriction were excluded (Dinkler et al., 2023). One limitation deserves emphasis: the data did not capture the fear presentation, so the estimate may not apply equally to all three presentations (Sanchez-Cerezo et al., 2024).
The finding does not stand alone. Food neophobia, the reluctance to try new foods, is strongly heritable in middle childhood: in 5,390 twin pairs aged 8–11, heritability was 0.78, non-shared environment accounted for the remaining 22%, and shared environment made no detectable contribution (Cooke et al., 2007). In infancy, appetite itself is heritable: among 2,402 twin pairs assessed during the first three months of life, while still exclusively milk-fed, heritability was 84% for slowness in eating, 72% for satiety responsiveness, 59% for food responsiveness and 53% for enjoyment of food (Llewellyn et al., 2010). These are among the traits that the three-dimensional model of ARFID links to its presentations (Thomas et al., 2017).


A window for the family
One study adds an important developmental nuance. In 1,921 families with twins aged 16 months, food fussiness was explained equally by genetic influences (0.46) and by environmental influences shared within the family (0.46), whereas for food neophobia the shared environment explained less (0.22) and genes more (0.58). The two traits largely shared their genetic and shared-environmental roots (Smith et al., 2017).
Set side by side (Figure 3.1), the studies suggest a pattern familiar from developmental behavioural genetics: in early childhood the family environment accounts for a substantial share of the differences between children in how selectively they eat, while by middle childhood that share has largely disappeared and genetic influences dominate. The comparison must be made with care, because the samples, ages and measures differ. But if the pattern holds, it identifies a window, roughly the second and third years of life, in which what happens at the family table makes the most difference to how fussy children are relative to one another.








Figure 3.1: Sources of variation in selective eating and ARFID in four twin studies. Each bar partitions individual differences into additive genetic (A), shared environmental (C) and non-shared environmental (E) components. Where only A and C were reported, E is shown as the remainder. Samples, ages and measures differ, so the bars are not directly comparable.







Five misreadings to avoid
Because heritability estimates are so often misread in public discussion, it is worth stating plainly what they do not mean.

Not a share of each child. A heritability of 0.79 does not mean that 79% of a particular child’s ARFID is caused by genes. It describes the sources of differences between children in a population.
Not fixed. Heritability is specific to the population and to the range of environments it experienced. A study of Swedish children born between 1992 and 2010 tells us about that population; a different food culture, health system or media environment could yield a different estimate.
Not a limit on change. A trait can be highly heritable and still shift substantially when the environment changes for everyone. Height is the classic example: highly heritable within generations, yet average height has changed markedly across generations as nutrition improved.
Not proof that the family does not matter. An estimate of zero for the shared environment means that growing up in the same family does not make siblings more alike on this trait. It does not mean that family environments have no effect; effects that differ between siblings in the same family are counted as non-shared.
Not immutability. Highly heritable conditions can respond to treatment. As Section 3.7 shows, ARFID does.

title: 3  Seed and soil: genetic and environmental determinants
text:
3.2 From twins to genomes
Twin studies estimate how much genes matter in aggregate; molecular studies try to identify which genetic variants are involved. For ARFID this work has only just begun. In a subsample of 5,157 autistic children from a large US autism cohort, ARFID risk was estimated at 21%, and at up to 17% among their parents. The narrow-sense heritability of ARFID risk was estimated at 0.45, and polygenic scores linked ARFID risk to the genetics of autism, neuroticism and metabolic syndrome (Koomar et al., 2021).
The first genome-wide study of avoidant/restrictive eating in a general population sample was published in 2026. Using the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study, it examined 35,751 children with maternal reports at ages 3 and 8, linked to national health registries. Broadly defined avoidant/restrictive eating was common and often transient: 17.7% of children showed it only at age 3, 8.4% only at age 8, and 6.0% at both ages. When at least one indicator of clinical significance (such as nutritional deficiency) was required, the corresponding figures were 3.2%, 1.4% and 1.8%. Children with persistent symptoms had more developmental difficulties across several domains. The heritability captured by common genetic variants ranged from 8% to 16%; two genome-wide significant loci were identified, including an association near ADCY3 for the clinically significant phenotype; and small to moderate genetic correlations were found with mental-health, cognitive and educational, anthropometric, food-related and gastrointestinal phenotypes (Bjørndal et al., 2026).
The gap between twin-based heritability (around 0.8) and the heritability captured by common variants (around 0.1) is typical of complex traits and should not be misread as room for the environment. It reflects, in part, the many small genetic effects that current samples cannot yet detect, rare variants that common-variant methods do not capture, and differences between phenotype definitions. Larger efforts are under way: ARFID-GEN aims to genotype 3,000 children and adults with ARFID (Bulik et al., 2023); the Eating Disorders Genetics Initiative 2 will recruit 20,000 participants across anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder and ARFID (Berthold et al., 2025); and the Swedish ARIES study will establish a national biobank and research registry of 1,500 children and adolescents with ARFID and 500 controls, combining genetic analyses with questionnaires on co-occurring conditions and parental stress and, in a subset, analyses of the gut microbiome (Hog et al., 2025). A review of what such work might deliver argues that clarifying the genomic architecture of ARFID, and its place in the landscape of other eating and mental disorders, will be a key step towards understanding its biological mechanisms (Kennedy et al., 2022).
For a book about environments, these studies matter for a methodological reason. Genetically informed designs are among the few tools that can separate an environmental cause from an environmental correlate. When parents who are themselves selective eaters raise children who become selective eaters, the association between family meals and child eating may reflect shared genes rather than learned behaviour. Only designs that measure or control genetic liability can tell the two apart.

title: 3  Seed and soil: genetic and environmental determinants
text:
3.3 The developmental soil
The first environment a child encounters is the developing body itself, and the evidence suggests that ARFID often grows out of a broader neurodevelopmental profile. In a Japanese birth cohort of 3,728 children assessed repeatedly from six months to three years, a composite score of early neurodevelopmental problems predicted suspected ARFID at ages 4–7: children in the highest risk percentiles had roughly three times the odds, and the absolute risk of later ARFID for children above the 90th percentile was 3.1%. Early problems with general development, communication and language, attention, social interaction and sleep were more predictive than early feeding problems, and the developmental trajectories of children with and without later ARFID began to diverge after their first birthday. Early feeding problems themselves were common and rarely developed into ARFID (Dinkler et al., 2022). Population data from Sweden (Section 2.4.1) and Norway (Bjørndal et al., 2026) point in the same direction.
Birth and early medical history may also matter. In a German clinical sample of 51 children with ARFID, those aged 0–5 had more often been born preterm, had experienced more pre- and perinatal complications and had undergone more invasive procedures after birth than those aged 6–17, and they had more physical conditions, particularly congenital anomalies (Brosig et al., 2023). The study is small and clinical, and it cannot separate cause from correlate. It is consistent, however, with a plausible pathway in which early medical experiences around the mouth and throat make eating aversive before a child has words to describe it.
The Norwegian data add a crucial qualification: most early avoidant/restrictive eating is transient (Bjørndal et al., 2026). The developmental question is therefore less “who starts?” than “who does not stop?”. The children whose difficulties persist appear to be those with broader developmental vulnerabilities, which is exactly where early recognition is most likely to help.

section: 3.4 The family table: practices, accommodation and feedback
text:
3.4 The family table: practices, accommodation and feedback

Who influences whom?
Parents of selective eaters often try to make their children eat, and pressure to eat is associated with more selective eating. For a long time this association was read as evidence that pressure causes fussiness. Longitudinal studies show that the causal arrow runs both ways. In the Dutch Generation R cohort of 4,845 mother–child pairs, fussy eating at ages 1½ and 3 predicted greater parental pressure at age 4; pressure at age 4 in turn predicted more fussiness at age 6, even after accounting for earlier fussiness. The path from child to parent was the stronger of the two (Jansen et al., 2017). A study of 853 families of preschool children in Shanghai likewise found that parental encouragement of healthy eating and content-restrictive feeding were bidirectionally associated with food fussiness (Wang et al., 2023). A systematic review of food neophobia had earlier identified parental pressure and the absence of encouragement or affection at mealtimes among associated factors (Torres et al., 2020).
The pattern is best understood as a feedback loop, and an analogy may help. Two dancers who keep stepping on each other’s feet are not usually helped by asking who started it. Each partner’s move is a response to the last move of the other, and the pattern is maintained by both. In behavioural genetics the same idea is called evocative gene–environment correlation: a child’s genetically influenced eating evokes parental responses, which then become part of that child’s environment and feed back on the eating. Parents who share some of their child’s genetic liability may also share some of the child’s food preferences, which complicates matters further.


Accommodation and its costs
The other side of pressure is accommodation: cooking separate meals, avoiding restaurants, carrying safe foods, rearranging family life around the restriction. Accommodation is an understandable response to a distressed child, and in the short term it reduces conflict. In childhood anxiety disorders it is thought to help maintain avoidance, and a parent-based treatment adapted from that field, SPACE-ARFID, targets it directly. In a pilot trial with the parents of 15 children aged 6–14, symptom severity, impairment and family accommodation all fell significantly, and parents and children rated the treatment as highly satisfactory (Shimshoni et al., 2020).
Families experience these loops from the inside. Parents of children with sensory sensitivities and picky eating describe a battle for control of the sensory environment, and the stigma and disapproval of others (Cunliffe et al., 2022); among adolescents in treatment, family functioning is impaired to a degree comparable to anorexia nervosa (Rienecke et al., 2026). None of this assigns blame. It identifies the family table as a place where small, repeated interactions can either tighten a loop or loosen it.

section: 3.5 Bodies that teach: aversive events, illness and the gut
text:
3.5 Bodies that teach: aversive events, illness and the gut

Learning to fear eating
The fear presentation of ARFID is the one in which an environmental trigger is most visible. Clinical series report histories of choking or vomiting in a substantial minority of patients (Fisher et al., 2014) and more fears of vomiting and choking in younger patients with ARFID than in those with other eating disorders (Nicely et al., 2014). A recent theoretical model draws a close parallel with panic disorder: the fear presentation typically begins with an unexpected aversive event, develops through catastrophic misinterpretation of the probability or significance of its recurrence, and is maintained by heightened attention to minor bodily sensations associated with the feared event (interoceptive sensitivity), rising anxiety and progressively wider avoidance (Zickgraf & Schwartz, 2025).
Neuroimaging studies support parts of this account. When young people viewed images specific to ARFID fears, such as choking and vomiting, the amygdala responded robustly across all participants, and those with the fear presentation showed a greater insula response than healthy controls. The authors suggest that universally feared experiences such as choking and vomiting may act as the unconditioned stimulus from which ARFID fear is learned, partly through the insular cortex, a region closely associated with the perception of internal bodily states (Sailer et al., 2025). A second study of 110 children, adolescents and young adults found that participants with ARFID showed greater activation than controls in regions associated with conflict monitoring, sensory association and motor preparation when viewing food, that the fear group showed greater amygdala activation, and that greater lack of interest was associated with lower activation of the hypothalamus, the brain’s central regulator of appetite (Thomas et al., 2025). These results map onto the three systems proposed by the dimensional model (Thomas et al., 2017), though they come from single centres and await replication. Structural imaging of children under 13 adds that ARFID and early-onset anorexia nervosa show distinct brain patterns despite similar body mass, and that the pattern in ARFID overlaps with that seen in autism (Moreau et al., 2025).


When the body is the environment
For many young people the environment that teaches restriction is their own gastrointestinal tract. Section 2.4.3 documented the high frequency of ARFID symptoms in gastrointestinal and immune-mediated conditions. The causal pathway is easy to imagine and hard to prove: real symptoms (pain, nausea, reflux, diarrhoea) make certain foods aversive; avoidance brings short-term relief; and avoidance generalises beyond what the illness requires. A conceptual model of the microbiota–gut–brain axis goes further, hypothesising that the narrow diet characteristic of ARFID reduces gut microbial diversity and that the resulting changes in microbial signalling may in turn affect appetite, reward, interoception, sensory sensitivity, disgust and fear learning (Schneider et al., 2024). The model is a set of testable hypotheses, not established fact, but it illustrates how a restricted diet could become part of the environment that maintains restriction.
Some triggers are acute and immune-related. Among 130 children and adolescents with pediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS), 56% developed abrupt-onset restriction of food intake during a flare, and the reasons they gave (selective eating, low appetite or interest, and fear of choking, vomiting or contamination) aligned with the three ARFID presentations (Kapphahn et al., 2025). A sudden onset of restriction in a previously flexible eater is a reason for medical as well as psychological assessment.

text:
3.6 The social and structural environment
The diagnostic criteria exclude restriction explained by the lack of available food, but that does not make poverty irrelevant. It means that food insecurity and ARFID must be distinguished, and that the instruments used to measure ARFID must work equally well in food-secure and food-insecure populations. One study found that they do: the NIAS and a measure of adult appetitive traits showed strong measurement invariance across food security status in three samples, so differences observed between food-secure and food-insecure groups are not artefacts of measurement (Ban et al., 2024). Direct evidence on the socio-economic distribution of ARFID remains scarce, and none of it yet comes from registers. In a weighted national survey of adolescents in the United States aged 10–17 years, food insecurity was associated with an 18% higher adjusted risk of what the authors classified as ARFID behaviours (Caouette et al., 2026); among more than 50,000 adults completing a self-selected online eating-disorder screen, those with a positive ARFID screen more often reported lower household income than most other diagnostic or risk groups (D’Adamo et al., 2023). Both studies are cross-sectional and rely on screening items rather than diagnosis, and neither can separate restriction imposed by scarcity, which the criteria exclude, from ARFID that coexists with it.


A gap worth closing. A targeted PubMed search (22 November 2026) combining ARFID with socioeconomic, deprivation, income, poverty or food insecurity returned 20 records, none of them a register study. Linking diagnosed cases to area-level deprivation indices would be the natural next design.
Culture matters too. Food repertoires, meal structures and norms about children’s eating differ widely, and a Latin American commentary argues that the diagnosis and treatment of ARFID have been framed largely within Western clinical frameworks, with assessment tools whose applicability across cultural contexts has rarely been tested (Trujillo-ChiVacuán, 2025). The Spanish adaptation of the NIAS in Mexican youth (Medina-Tepal et al., 2023) is a step in that direction, but, as Section 1.6 noted, no comparable work exists for Spanish adolescents.

section: 3.7 Is the environment a lever? Evidence from treatment
text:
3.7 Is the environment a lever? Evidence from treatment

What lights a fire and what keeps it burning
Observational studies can show that environments are associated with ARFID; only interventions can show that changing an environment changes the course of the disorder. Here an analogy is helpful. What lights a fire and what keeps it burning are different questions: a match is needed to start it, oxygen to sustain it. Treatment trials say little about the match, because they begin after onset, but they are the best evidence available about the oxygen.


The trials so far
The first fully powered randomised controlled trial in ARFID was published in 2026. Ninety-eight underweight children aged 6–12 were randomised to 14 telehealth sessions over four months of either family-based treatment adapted for ARFID (FBT-ARFID), in which parents take charge of re-nourishing their child, or an individual psychoeducational and motivational therapy. FBT-ARFID was superior in restoring weight. The two treatments did not differ in their effect on overall ARFID symptom severity, but exploratory analyses suggested that the most severely affected children improved more with the family-based approach (Lock et al., 2026). In end-of-treatment sessions from that trial, parents described progress beyond weight, including greater dietary variety, less fear around eating and more flexibility at meals, as well as increased confidence in managing ARFID themselves (Datta et al., 2026).
Cognitive-behavioural therapy for ARFID (CBT-AR), a manualised outpatient treatment that works on the specific driver of restriction through, among other things, graded exposure to novel or feared foods, has been tested in open trials (Thomas et al., 2018). Among 20 children and adolescents aged 10–17 who began treatment, clinicians rated 85% as much or very much improved; patients added an average of 16.7 new foods; the underweight subgroup gained weight; and 70% no longer met diagnostic criteria at the end of treatment (Thomas et al., 2020). A similar open trial supported its feasibility in adults (Thomas et al., 2021). In a pooled analysis of 94 patients aged 10–55, the presence of the fear presentation predicted an almost threefold greater likelihood of remission, whereas age, weight status, sex and the sensory or lack-of-interest presentations did not predict outcome (Palmer et al., 2025), a finding that echoes the better natural course of fear-driven ARFID described in Section 2.2.2. Treatments derived from panic disorder have been proposed specifically for the fear presentation (Zickgraf & Schwartz, 2025), and the parent-based approach described in Section 3.4.2 offers a route for children who will not engage directly (Shimshoni et al., 2020).
The evidence remains modest: one fully powered trial, several open trials and pilots, and outcomes concentrated on weight and symptom severity. But it is enough to establish the point that matters for this chapter. A disorder with a heritability near 0.8 responds to interventions that work entirely through the environment: through what parents do at meals, through graded experience with feared and novel foods, through the reinterpretation of bodily sensations. Heritability and modifiability are answers to different questions.






ImportantFor practice




Avoid pressure; plan exposure. Pressure to eat tends to backfire; gradual, predictable exposure to new or feared foods is the shared ingredient of the treatments with the best evidence.
Notice accommodation. Separate meals and safe-food routines are understandable, but they can maintain avoidance. Reducing them is best done gradually and with professional support.
Watch after an aversive event. A choking, vomiting or painful episode followed by expanding avoidance warrants early attention; fear-driven ARFID responds comparatively well to treatment.
Look at the whole child. Early feeding problems are common and usually pass; persistence alongside broader developmental difficulties is the stronger signal.

text:
3.8 A working model
The evidence reviewed in this chapter can be drawn together in a simple working model (Figure 3.2). It distinguishes three layers, colour-coded in the figure: liability (blue), which is largely genetic and neurodevelopmental and shapes how sensitive a child is to sensory input, how strong their appetite is and how readily threat systems are engaged; triggers (ochre), such as aversive eating events and medical illness, which can set restriction in motion; and maintaining loops (violet), in which restriction and its consequences feed back on themselves through avoidance and interoceptive sensitivity, through parental pressure and accommodation, and through the nutritional and possibly microbial effects of a narrow diet.

The model has a clear implication for Chapter 4. Digital environments are unlikely to touch the liability layer, which is set early and largely genetically. If they matter, they will matter as triggers and as maintaining loops: by exposing young people repeatedly to vicarious versions of the aversive events that teach fear, by supplying information that shapes how parents respond at the table, and by reinforcing avoidance and attention to bodily sensations. Each of these possibilities is graded H at present. The next chapter asks how they might be tested.






NoteKey points




Twin studies estimate the heritability of ARFID at about 0.8, with the rest of the variation due to environments unique to each child; related traits such as food neophobia and infant appetite are also strongly heritable.
Heritability describes differences in a population, not causes in an individual, and it is compatible with large environmental effects and with effective treatment.
In early childhood, the shared family environment explains a substantial share of differences in food fussiness; by middle childhood that share has largely disappeared.
The first population genome-wide study found that most early avoidant/restrictive eating is transient, that persistence goes with broader developmental difficulties, and that common genetic variants capture 8–16% of the variation.
Parental pressure and child selectivity influence each other; aversive events, illness and accommodation help to trigger and maintain restriction; and treatments that change these environments help, especially for fear-driven ARFID.

3  Seed and soil: genetic and environmental determinants

title: 4  Digital soil: social platforms, recommender systems and ARFID
text:
4.1 What is established: the body-image pathway
There is an old story about a man searching for his keys under a streetlamp. Asked whether he dropped them there, he says no, he dropped them in the park, but this is where the light is. Research on digital media and eating disorders has a streetlamp problem. Two decades of work have lit up one pathway thoroughly: from idealised images, through social comparison and the internalisation of appearance ideals, to body dissatisfaction and disordered eating. That pathway is real and well documented, and Section 4.1 reviews it. But it was mapped for disorders defined by concern about weight and shape, and ARFID is defined by the absence of that concern (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). If digital environments matter for ARFID, the keys are probably somewhere else.
The chapter proceeds in six steps. Section 4.1 summarises the evidence on the body-image pathway, including what platforms themselves deliver to young users. Section 4.2 explains why that evidence does not transfer to ARFID and measures, with a reproducible bibliometric check, how little light falls on it. Section 4.3 sets out seven candidate digital pathways as testable hypotheses and grades each, using a small simulation to make one mechanism concrete. Section 4.4 asks how digital exposure can be measured, Section 4.5 asks what current regulation does and does not reach, and Section 4.6 proposes a research agenda. Throughout, the working model of Section 3.8 provides the frame: digital environments are unlikely to alter the largely genetic liability layer, so if they matter for ARFID they will act as triggers and as maintaining loops.

4  Digital soil: social platforms, recommender systems and ARFID

title: 4  Digital soil: social platforms, recommender systems and ARFID
text:
Associations and their size
The first systematic review of social networking sites and eating outcomes identified 20 studies and concluded that use of these sites was associated with body-image concern and disordered eating. Photo-related activities were singled out as particularly problematic, and in the few studies that examined process, appearance-based social comparison mediated the association. Nearly all the evidence was correlational (Holland & Tiggemann, 2016). Later reviews broadened the picture without overturning it. A scoping review of 50 studies from 17 countries, covering people aged 10–24 and published between 2016 and 2021, found consistent links running through social comparison, internalisation of thin or fit ideals and self-objectification, strengthened by pro-eating-disorder content and appearance-focused platforms. Of its 45 quantitative studies, however, 30 were cross-sectional and only two were longitudinal (Dane & Bhatia, 2023). A review restricted to preadolescents and adolescents (16 studies) reached a similar conclusion and noted the same reliance on cross-sectional self-report (Digennaro & Tescione, 2024).
Meta-analyses put numbers on these associations, and the pattern of the numbers is instructive (Table 4.1). Across 22 studies contributing 87 effect sizes, the correlation between use of social networking sites and disordered eating behaviours was small (r = 0.09) (Zhang et al., 2021). Problematic use of the internet, which measures compulsive or impairing use rather than time, correlated more strongly with eating-disorder psychopathology (r = 0.22 in 32,295 participants), and the association was not moderated by gender (Ioannidis et al., 2021). The strongest associations concern a psychological process rather than an exposure: across 83 studies and 55,440 participants, online social comparison correlated r = 0.45 with body-image concern and r = 0.36 with eating-disorder symptoms (Bonfanti et al., 2025).
The gradient, small for time and moderate for process, is the first lesson of this literature. How wet one gets depends less on the hours spent outdoors than on whether one is standing under the gutter.


Content matters more than time
Studies that separate what young people see from how long they spend online support the same conclusion. In two demographically diverse cohorts of undergraduates surveyed in 2015 and 2022, the type of content consumed, but not the time spent on social media or the number of platforms used, was associated with body-image disturbance and disordered eating once gender and body mass index were taken into account. Exposure to weight-loss content was associated with lower body appreciation, greater fear of negative appearance evaluation and more frequent binge eating; contrary to the authors’ hypothesis, body-positivity and body-neutrality content was not protective (Sanzari et al., 2023).
Experimental studies isolate content effects more cleanly. A systematic review of 43 experiments (N = 8,637; 89.6% female; mean age 21.6) found that viewing idealised images on social networking sites increased body dissatisfaction, that comparison made while viewing mediated the effect, and that a stable tendency to compare oneself with others moderated it; only two of the experiments involved adolescents (Fioravanti et al., 2022). In a systematic review of “fitspiration” content, 17 of the 19 studies that examined body image found that exposure increased body dissatisfaction (Jerónimo & Carraça, 2022). In a randomised online experiment with women with (n = 172) and without (n = 210) eating disorders, 30 Instagram posts of fitspiration increased body dissatisfaction, whereas body-positive posts and text-based “body neutrality” posts reduced it; the effects did not differ between the two groups (Ladwig et al., 2024). Side-by-side “Instagram vs reality” images reduced body dissatisfaction in 305 women aged 18–30 relative to idealised images alone, and blunted the effect of appearance comparison (Tiggemann & Anderberg, 2020). A systematic review and meta-analysis of 56 studies concluded that body-positive content improves body satisfaction and mood in the short term, with weaker effects on body surveillance and social comparison (Jiménez-García et al., 2025).
Individual differences shape these effects. In 1,153 adolescents (55.4% boys; mean age 13.7), internalisation of the thin ideal was the only variable associated with body dissatisfaction in both sexes once other factors were considered, and among boys internalisation of a muscular ideal moderated the link with social media: for boys who had strongly internalised that ideal, more use went with greater dissatisfaction (Vuong et al., 2021). Among 246 early-adolescent girls, media literacy, particularly critical thinking about media, buffered the effects of thin-ideal internalisation and habitual upward comparison on body satisfaction after exposure to thin-ideal images (McLean et al., 2016).
A smaller literature concerns content about food rather than bodies. A systematic review of 38 studies found positive associations between exposure to some eating-related content (fast-food advertising, “clean eating” and eating videos) and body-image concern, disordered eating and consumption, but no such association for “healthy food” content; viewers expressed mixed feelings about nutrition information and mukbang videos, in which hosts eat large quantities of food on camera (Wu et al., 2024). A content analysis of 250 TikTok videos from the five most popular diet-related hashtags found that more than half depicted body checking and more than half offered dietary advice. Most of the advice-givers (64%) presented themselves as experts, but claimed expertise was not associated with engagement; humour was. Only 6.4% of videos depicted disordered eating behaviours outright (Munro et al., 2024). The point for this book is that a large share of food content online is advice: confident, personal and often unqualified.


Within-person evidence and causal tests
Most of the evidence above compares people with one another. Two longitudinal studies that separated between-person from within-person effects in adolescents complicate the picture. In a three-wave panel of 2,500 Czech adolescents aged 11–16, adolescents who were more active around appearance on social media were more dissatisfied with their bodies, but increases in an individual’s appearance activity did not predict increases in that individual’s body dissatisfaction six months later, and neither internalisation nor comparison mediated the link within persons (Kvardova et al., 2025). In another within-person study of adolescents, increased posting predicted lower body dissatisfaction four months later in one interval only, increased exposure predicted lower dissatisfaction among boys, and liking or commenting predicted nothing (Schreurs & Vandenbosch, 2022). These findings do not cancel the experimental evidence for short-term effects. They do caution against reading population correlations as descriptions of what happens inside each adolescent, the same distinction between populations and individuals that Section 3.1.3 drew for heritability.
Causal tests of reducing use are now accumulating. Meta-analyses of randomised trials in which participants were asked to stop using social media for a period have found modest benefits for mental health in adults and adolescents (Linden, 2026). A recent study of young adults aged 18–24 illustrates both the promise and the limits of this evidence: among 295 participants who opted into a one-week “detox”, symptoms of depression fell by 24.8%, anxiety by 16.1% and insomnia by 14.5%, while loneliness did not change; but participation was optional and there was no control group, so expectation effects and regression to the mean cannot be excluded (Calvert et al., 2025). Eating outcomes were not measured.


What platforms deliver
Studies of users measure what people report seeing. A second body of evidence examines what platforms deliver, and most of it comes from audits by advocacy organisations, investigative journalism and leaked or disclosed company documents. These sources call for explicit appraisal, and they are graded here accordingly.
In the Deadly by Design audit, researchers created two new TikTok accounts registered as 13-year-olds in each of the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada. One account in each pair had a username containing “loseweight”. All accounts paused on and liked videos about body image and mental health, and the first 30 minutes of each “For You” feed were recorded. Eating-disorder content appeared within eight minutes at the earliest, and body-image or mental-health content was recommended every 39 seconds. The report’s headline finding was that the “vulnerable” accounts were shown three times as many harmful videos and twelve times as many self-harm videos as the standard accounts (Center for Countering Digital Hate, 2022). The report’s own tables show that the threefold difference was driven by self-harm and suicide content (74 videos against 6); for eating-disorder videos the difference was small (35 against 29). The distinction matters for what follows.
A later audit of YouTube used an account set up as a 13-year-old girl in the United States, seeded with 100 eating-disorder videos found through 20 search terms, and recorded the top ten “Up Next” recommendations in 100 separate simulations. Of the 1,000 recommendations, 638 concerned eating disorders or weight loss, 344 were classified as harmful eating-disorder content and 50 concerned self-harm or suicide; the harmful videos averaged more than 388,000 views each, and YouTube took no action on 81 of 100 such videos that the researchers reported (Center for Countering Digital Hate, 2024). On Pinterest, a single click on a pin about recovery from an eating disorder was enough, in each of ten fresh test accounts, for four to eight of the first 25 pins in the home feed to concern weight loss or eating disorders (Golbeck, 2025). For recommenders, seeking recovery and seeking the disorder can look alike. A follower-network analysis of Instagram by Reset Australia mapped a “bubble” of pro-eating-disorder accounts (Reset Australia, 2022), which other researchers have summarised as reaching some 20 million unique followers (Center for Countering Digital Hate, 2022). A legal analysis also describes a newspaper investigation in which a dozen automated accounts registered as 13-year-olds were served tens of thousands of weight-loss videos within a few weeks (Costello et al., 2023).
The most informative single document comes from inside a platform. In an internal study disclosed in 2025, Meta followed 1,149 teenagers in the United States through the 2023–2024 school year and manually reviewed random samples of the content they were shown over three months. For the 223 teenagers who reported frequently feeling bad about their bodies after using Instagram, content the company labelled body-focused or “eating-disorder adjacent” made up 10.5% of what they saw, against 3.3% for the 795 other teenagers in the comparison. A broader class of content that Meta’s advisers had supported limiting made up 27.3% and 13.6% respectively (Horwitz, 2025b; Meta Platforms, 2024). Only three of the flagged pieces in either group scored above a low threshold on the company’s existing integrity classifiers, which had been built to detect policy violations rather than this kind of material (Meta Platforms, 2024). The authors stated that the causal direction could not be established: teenagers who felt bad about their bodies may have sought such content out (Horwitz, 2025b). A separate report by child-safety organisations, reviewed by researchers at Northeastern University, judged only 8 of 47 Instagram teen-safety features to be fully effective; Meta disputed the findings (Horwitz, 2025a).
Figure 4.1 sets the two sources that compare groups side by side.








Figure 4.1: Exposure gradients: how much more of each content category was delivered to ‘vulnerable’ users than to comparison users in two sources. Points show the ratio of the two values (logarithmic scale); labels give the underlying figures. In the TikTok audit, vulnerability was signalled by a username containing ‘loseweight’ and all accounts behaved identically; in the Instagram study, groups were defined by teenagers’ own reports of frequent body dissatisfaction, so causal direction cannot be inferred. The ratios are descriptive, not estimates of harm.





These sources share well-known weaknesses. Audits use few accounts and short observation windows; classifications are made by the organisations’ own researchers (in the YouTube audit, each decision was agreed by at least two of them); the organisations campaign on the issues they study; and platforms change their systems continually, so findings are dated snapshots. None of the figures is a prevalence estimate. Yet the audits establish something that surveys of users cannot: conditional delivery, the fact that a signal of interest or vulnerability changes what the system serves. The internal Meta study adds the platform’s own measurement, with an appropriately cautious reading of causal direction. Taken together, the evidence supports, at grade E2, the claim that recommender systems deliver more eating-disorder-relevant content to young users who signal interest or vulnerability. Whether that delivery causes the onset of an eating disorder remains H.
The same platforms also offer support. For adolescents with eating disorders, social media has been described as a double-edged sword: a source of connection, information and recovery communities, and also of triggers, comparison and “thinspiration” (Nawaz et al., 2024). Because adolescents are unlikely to stop using these platforms, reviews of mitigation strategies argue that harm reduction has to work within them (Mazzeo et al., 2024). A case report describes how videos meant to warn against anorexia (labelled “anti-pro-ana”) led an adolescent to imitate the behaviours they depicted (Logrieco et al., 2021). In Spain, a small cross-sectional study of 115 students aged 12–17 at one school in Córdoba classified 43.5% as at risk of an eating disorder and found that more hours of social media use were associated with higher risk (odds ratio 5.54) (Peréz-Jiménez et al., 2025). The design does not allow causal inference, but it is a reminder that the question is also being asked locally.

title: 4  Digital soil: social platforms, recommender systems and ARFID
section: 4.2 Why ARFID falls outside that evidence
text:
4.2 Why ARFID falls outside that evidence

A definitional exclusion
The pathway just described runs through appearance comparison, internalisation of ideals and body dissatisfaction, and its outcome measures (body dissatisfaction, drive for thinness, dietary restraint) are designed to capture concern about weight and shape. ARFID is defined by the absence of that concern as the driver of restriction (American Psychiatric Association, 2022), and measures that separate the two families of motivation exist precisely because the distinction matters clinically (Çelik et al., 2026). The meta-analytic findings of Section 4.1 therefore cannot simply be transferred to ARFID.
The boundary is not watertight. A nine-year-old with ARFID and severe malnutrition valued her small size and described a desire for thinness shaped by beauty ideals on social media, yet her restriction was driven by low appetite, fear of new foods and fear of adverse consequences (Barney et al., 2022). In 515 adults recruited online, dysmorphic concern fully mediated the association between avoidant/restrictive eating and suicidal ideation (Salameh et al., 2024); the design was cross-sectional and the eating measure a screen, but the finding suggests that body concern can co-occur with ARFID and matter for a subgroup. Neither observation licenses the transfer of body-image findings to ARFID. Neither licenses the opposite conclusion either, that ARFID is untouched by digital life.


How little light: a bibliometric check
How much of the research on social media concerns ARFID can be checked directly. On 21 November 2026, PubMed was searched for records published from 2013 (the year ARFID entered DSM-5) whose titles or abstracts named each condition, first alone and then together with any of six social-media terms. Figure 4.2 shows the results.








Figure 4.2: Records in PubMed combining each condition with social-media terms, 2013 to 21 November 2026. Bars show the number of records (logarithmic scale); labels give the number combining the condition with social-media terms, the number naming the condition at all, and the share. Search strings: [condition terms][tiab] AND (“social media”[tiab] OR TikTok[tiab] OR Instagram[tiab] OR YouTube[tiab] OR Facebook[tiab] OR “social networking”[tiab]), with publication date from 2013. Condition terms: “body image”; “anorexia nervosa”; “bulimia nervosa”; “binge eating disorder” OR “binge-eating disorder”; orthorexia OR “orthorexia nervosa”; ARFID OR “avoidant/restrictive food intake” OR “avoidant restrictive food intake”. Counts depend on the terms chosen (for example, records using only ‘pro-ana’ are not captured) and are an indicator, not a census.





The proportions are not the main point: ARFID’s share (1.5%) is in fact higher than that of anorexia nervosa (0.5%), whose literature is dominated by clinical and biological work. The point is the absolute volume and, above all, what the records do. Screening the abstracts of the 14 ARFID records shows that most use platforms as a means rather than study them as an object (Table 4.2). Nine name social media only as a recruitment or dissemination channel or as a keyword. Two measured media use in general samples of adolescents without analysing ARFID separately. Two are case reports in which content from social media is mentioned, one of them a case of orthorexia in which ARFID had been considered and excluded. One analysed platform content about ARFID: a study of pro-recovery videos on TikTok that included the hashtag #arfidrecovery (Greene et al., 2023). On the evidence of their abstracts, none reported an analysis of digital exposure specific to ARFID, and none tested an association with the onset or course of the disorder.

There is an irony here. Platforms have become part of the infrastructure of ARFID research: an international survey of people with eating disorders, advertised through social media, online forums and clinical services, recruited 6,612 respondents, 589 of whom reported a diagnosis of ARFID (Rodan et al., 2025), and much population data on ARFID now comes from online panels and online recruitment (Chapter 1). The platforms help researchers find people with ARFID but are almost never what is being studied. That raises a further, methodological caution: people recruited through platforms may differ systematically from those who are not, including in exactly the digital habits that this chapter is concerned with.

title: 4  Digital soil: social platforms, recommender systems and ARFID
text:
4.3 Candidate digital pathways
If the keys are not under the body-image lamp, where might they be? This section proposes seven places to look. Each is stated as a hypothesis, linked to the presentation of ARFID it would most plausibly affect (the three dials of Section 2.2.1: sensory sensitivity, lack of interest, fear of aversive consequences) and graded. Table 4.3 draws them together at the end.

Vicarious aversive content and fear learning
The fear presentation of ARFID often begins with an aversive eating event. In a multi-site clinical study, a history of vomiting or choking was recorded in 13.2% of young people with ARFID (Fisher et al., 2014), and a recent theoretical model compares the course of the fear presentation with that of panic disorder (Zickgraf & Schwartz, 2025). In functional imaging, images of choking and vomiting elicited amygdala responses across young people, with greater insula activation in those with the fear presentation; the authors suggest that universally feared experiences of this kind may act as the unconditioned stimulus from which ARFID fear is learnt (Sailer et al., 2025). Not every patient, however, recalls a frightening event of their own.
Experimental psychology offers a route by which fear can be acquired without direct experience. Forty years of research show that fears can be learnt vicariously, by watching other people’s responses (Askew & Field, 2008). In children, pairing pictures of novel animals with fearful faces increased fear beliefs, avoidance, heart rate and attentional bias towards the animals, and the changes in beliefs and avoidance persisted at one week and one month (Reynolds et al., 2014). Fear also spread second-hand: animals merely seen alongside the fear-paired animal acquired fear-related responses, which the authors suggest may explain why some people cannot recall any learning episode for their fears (Reynolds et al., 2017). In 60 children aged 6–10, peers were as effective as adults in transmitting fear, and later pairing with positive faces reduced it (Dunne & Askew, 2018). A systematic review of 18 experiments found that positive modelling prevented, reduced or reversed fear in most of them (Krause & Askew, 2022).
Hypothesis. Short-form video makes vicarious aversive eating events abundant: people choking, gagging, vomiting, reacting to food poisoning or allergens, or warning that a food is dangerous. For a child or adolescent with a sensitive threat system, each such video may function as a vicarious learning trial, and repeated recommendation multiplies the trials. Second-order learning would allow fear to spread from the food shown to foods associated with it. The same literature suggests the converse: content showing calm peers eating varied food could act as positive modelling, which is one reason why a purely restrictive response to online content may be the wrong one. Grade: E2 for vicarious fear learning in children, with non-food stimuli and in the laboratory; H for the digital route to ARFID. The laboratory paradigms used pictures of animals and faces, not videos of eating, and that gap is exactly what research would need to close.


Gut-health, elimination diets and wellness advice
Gastrointestinal conditions are closely associated with ARFID. The association appears in population data (Flack et al., 2026), ARFID symptoms were found in 19% of patients with coeliac disease or non-coeliac gluten sensitivity at consultation (Atkins et al., 2026), and in inflammatory bowel disease positive screens were associated with lower food literacy (Yin et al., 2023). Online, people with gut symptoms meet a large volume of dietary advice from creators who present themselves as experts (Munro et al., 2024), alongside what one commentator calls “wellness scams” (Linden, 2026).
Hypothesis. Advice to eliminate foods in response to symptoms narrows the diet. In people who already attend closely to bodily sensations, the interoceptive sensitivity that the panic-disorder model places at the centre of fear-driven ARFID (Zickgraf & Schwartz, 2025), content attributing symptoms to particular foods may supply the catastrophic interpretations that maintain avoidance. Grade: E2 for the clinical association between gastrointestinal illness and ARFID; H for the digital route.


“Clean eating” and orthorexic ideals
A systematic review of 22 studies, mostly cross-sectional and in non-clinical samples, found that greater social media use was associated with more symptoms of orthorexia nervosa, particularly where content concerned nutrition, thinness and exercise, with stronger associations for Instagram, Tumblr and Grindr (Vintró-Alcaraz et al., 2026). A case report shows how the boundary with ARFID is drawn in practice: a 13-year-old with rapid weight loss was first thought to have anorexia nervosa, then ARFID, which was excluded because she showed no food avoidance as such; her restriction followed rules about nutrition taken from magazines and social media promoting an almost exclusively vegetable diet (Yoshimura et al., 2023). Proposed criteria for orthorexia remain provisional (Donini et al., 2022).
Hypothesis. Moralised categories of food (“clean”, “toxic”, “processed”) narrow the range of acceptable foods for reasons that are neither sensory nor appetitive. Where fear of contamination or illness enters, the restriction can come to resemble the fear presentation of ARFID. The practical implication is diagnostic: digital content may push some presentations towards this boundary, so screening and referral must ask why a young person avoids a food, not only what they avoid (Chapter 5). Grade: E1 for the cross-sectional association between social media use and orthorexic symptoms; E3 for boundary cases relevant to ARFID.


Diagnostic identity and online communities
Diagnosis-specific communities form around hashtags. A thematic analysis of 241 popular pro-recovery videos on TikTok under five hashtags, among them #arfidrecovery, found clear differences in how recovery was imagined from one diagnosis to the next (Greene et al., 2023). A content analysis of 100 TikTok videos on depression and anxiety, each viewed more than a million times, found that videos presenting personal experience attracted more engagement than videos by health professionals, and that mention of a professional diagnosis was the least common topic; the authors warn that attributing generic symptoms to a condition may encourage self-diagnosis (Samuel et al., 2024).
For ARFID the potential benefits are real. Recognition is poor, adults often go undiagnosed (Section 2.5.3), and parents of selective eaters gather in online support groups (Cunliffe et al., 2022). Communities may be where people first find a name for their difficulties and the confidence to seek help. The potential harms are equally plausible: ordinary picky eating relabelled as a disorder, an identity consolidated around a list of “safe foods”, accommodation normalised as the only kind response, or a presentation driven by weight concern presented, and accepted, as ARFID. Grade: E3 for the existence and character of ARFID content; H for its effects on help-seeking and course.


Diagnostic overshadowing, human and algorithmic
Diagnostic overshadowing occurs when a salient explanation leads observers to miss another. The dominant body-image frame can lead adults to overlook restriction that has nothing to do with weight, or to read co-occurring body concerns as the cause of restriction that they do not drive (Barney et al., 2022). The same frame is now being written into software. Methods for detecting eating disorders from social media content (content tags, topic modelling and natural-language processing) have been reviewed with the conclusion that they are feasible but that platforms’ moderation systems are opaque and need input from eating-disorder experts (D’Adamo et al., 2026). Large language models have been used to identify diet and body concerns in online communities (Chu et al., 2024). Such systems learn from the vocabulary of the communities on which they are trained, and that vocabulary is overwhelmingly about bodies. Their performance can also be uneven in ways that are hard to predict: in Spanish-language Twitter data from 177 users with signs of anorexia nervosa and 326 controls, classifiers missed far more cases among women (false-negative rate 0.082) than among men (0.005) (Solans Noguero et al., 2023). The internal Meta study adds that classifiers built to detect rule violations captured almost none of the body-focused material that human reviewers flagged (Meta Platforms, 2024). Content relevant to ARFID (videos of choking, lists of “safe foods”, complaints about textures) does not appear among the categories described in any of the documents reviewed here.
Hypothesis. The body-image frame produces systematic under-recognition of ARFID by people and by automated systems alike. Grade: E3. This is the pathway most directly relevant to Chapter 5, because a protocol based on a large language model could reproduce the same blind spot unless it is designed and tested against it.


Recommender amplification and the “bubble” effect
Engagement-optimised recommender systems learn from implicit signals such as how long a user lingers on an item. The audits described above used exactly such signals (accounts “paused briefly” on videos and liked them) and found that the feed adapted within minutes (Center for Countering Digital Hate, 2022). A young person whose attention is captured by threat-relevant content (and attentional bias towards feared stimuli is one of the effects of vicarious fear learning (Reynolds et al., 2014)) supplies the signal that such systems reward. Desire paths across a lawn offer an analogy: each crossing flattens the grass a little, which makes the same route more likely next time, until the path becomes the route. A recommender can wear a path in one user’s feed in the same way.
Figure 4.3 makes the mechanism explicit with a deliberately simple simulation. A feed draws 20 items per session from ten topics in proportion to learnt weights, with 10% of slots reserved for exploration. The user engages with each item with probability 0.30, except for one topic, here food-fear videos, where the probability is multiplied by an attraction ratio r. After each session, the weights decay by 10% and increase by one unit for each engagement. Nothing in the model is harmful by design: there is no malicious actor, no policy-violating content and no intention to narrow the feed.


Show the simulation code (R)
simulate_feed <- function(r, cap = NA, K = 10, sessions = 60, n_feed = 20,
                          p0 = 0.30, eta = 1, lambda = 0.90, eps = 0.10) {
  w <- rep(1, K); share <- numeric(sessions)
  for (t in seq_len(sessions)) {
    pr <- (1 - eps) * w / sum(w) + eps / K            # exploitation plus exploration
    if (!is.na(cap) && pr[1] > cap) {                  # optional exposure cap on topic 1
      pr[-1] <- pr[-1] / sum(pr[-1]) * (1 - cap); pr[1] <- cap }
    share[t] <- pr[1]
    feed <- sample.int(K, n_feed, replace = TRUE, prob = pr)
    p <- rep(p0, K); p[1] <- min(1, p0 * r)            # attraction ratio for topic 1
    eng <- rbinom(n_feed, 1, p[feed])                  # implicit engagement (dwell, like)
    w <- pmax(lambda * w + eta * tabulate(feed[eng == 1], nbins = K), 1e-6)
  }
  share
}
set.seed(2026)
runs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(list(list(r = 1, cap = NA), list(r = 1.15, cap = NA), list(r = 1.3, cap = NA),
                                   list(r = 1.5, cap = NA), list(r = 1.5, cap = 0.15)), function(s) {
  m <- replicate(500, simulate_feed(s$r, s$cap))
  data.frame(session = seq_len(nrow(m)), mean = rowMeans(m),
             lo = apply(m, 1, quantile, 0.10), hi = apply(m, 1, quantile, 0.90),
             r = s$r, policy = ifelse(is.na(s$cap), "Engagement only", "Engagement with 15% cap"))
}))










Figure 4.3: A stylised simulation of recommender amplification. Each line shows the mean share of a feed devoted to one topic (for example, food-fear videos) over 60 sessions, across 500 simulated users, when users engage with that topic r times as often as with nine others. The shaded band shows the 10th to 90th percentiles for r = 1.5. The dashed line shows the same user (r = 1.5) when the platform caps exposure to the topic at 15%, which is possible only if the topic is recognised as sensitive. Parameters are illustrative, not estimated from any platform.





Three features of the result are worth noting. First, a modest difference in attention is enough: with an attraction ratio of 1.3, the topic’s share of the feed nearly triples, and at 1.5 it reaches almost half the feed by the sixtieth session. Second, even a user with no particular attraction (r = 1) can drift: the mean stays at 10%, but individual feeds wander widely by chance, which is why “lock-in” can occur without any initial vulnerability. Third, an exposure cap holds the share down, but only if the content falls in a category that the platform recognises as sensitive. Food-fear content would not be capped by rules written for “eating-disorder content” in the body-image sense, and for such content the dashed line would simply coincide with the solid one.
The simulation shows that the mechanism is possible and how little it requires. It does not show that it operates on any particular platform, still less that it causes ARFID. Grade: E2 for the amplification of eating-disorder content by recommenders; H for content relevant to ARFID.


The parental information environment
Section 3.4 showed that parental pressure and a child’s selectivity influence each other over time (Jansen et al., 2017), and that accommodation can maintain avoidance (Shimshoni et al., 2020). Parents increasingly look for feeding advice online. In an Australian survey of 330 parents of children aged 2–5 with feeding concerns, 53.9% were concerned about fussy eating; online formats (websites, email, Facebook) were the preferred route for help, and 42.7% said they would take part in an online programme for more than 12 weeks (Boswell et al., 2019). A qualitative study of 29 caregivers in China found that digital information environments could either support or undermine healthy feeding, and identified misleading online information among the influences that sustained less healthy practices (Tan et al., 2026).
Hypothesis. The advice parents meet online can push them towards pressure (“no pudding until the plate is clean”) or towards accommodation (“just let them have their safe foods”), both of which are implicated in maintaining selective eating. The quality of advice about ARFID specifically has not been studied. Grade: E3 for parents’ reliance on online sources; H for effects on ARFID trajectories. The parental pathway also points to an opportunity: evidence-based guidance delivered where parents already look.

4.4 Measuring digital exposure
Testing these hypotheses requires measuring what people actually encounter online, and the dominant measure, self-reported time, is the weakest. The evidence reviewed above points to content and process rather than time (Bonfanti et al., 2025; Sanzari et al., 2023), and self-reports of time online are known to be imprecise. The last row is new. Under Article 40 of the Digital Services Act (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022), vetted researchers can request access to non-public data from very large online platforms and search engines to study systemic risks in the European Union. The delegated regulation that sets out the procedures was adopted on 2 July 2025 and entered into force on 29 October 2025, together with a data access portal (European Commission, 2025a). The systemic risks defined in Article 34 of the Act include negative effects on the protection of minors and serious negative consequences for people’s physical and mental well-being (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2022), so questions about ARFID-relevant content could in principle be framed as eligible research. No study has yet done so.
Every one of these designs raises ethical questions when the population is young. Audits should use adult personas wherever the question allows; exposure experiments with fear-relevant stimuli should begin in adults and include positive-modelling conditions; and data donation by minors involves consent, assent and data-protection requirements that vary by country (in Spain, for example, the age of digital consent is 14 (Jefatura del Estado, 2018)). None of these obstacles is insurmountable, but each needs to be designed in from the start.
